Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the hon. Finance Minister (Mr. White) on the impartial manner in which he has presented the budget to the House. It is the first time in the history of Canada, as I understand, that we have had the announcement of a surplus of $39,000,000. I observe that my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean) last night expressed himself as being very anxious to have $10,000,000 expended on the defence of the empire. I hope before I get through my remarks to be able to convince the Minister of Finance that there are many other places to put that $39,000,000 instead of contributing it to the defence of the empire; I mean by a lowering of taxation as much as possible. We have heard during this present session many arguments on protection pro and con, and from many of the remarks made I for one have come to the conclusion that self-interest seems to have priority over the interest of the masses of the community. A well-read man might believe that we have gone back to ancient history, as some of the arguments used during this debate were put forward almost in the same form as far back as the fifth century.

The protection of Trusts, which is the furnishing to the few the means of getting rich at the expense of the community at large, is nothing new and will continue I suppose as long as the masses which compose this nation allow themselves to be misled into the' belief that their interests rest on such a policy.
It is a well-known fact among those who are accustomed to gauge public opinion that this so-called protection as presented is not so popular amongst the masses as it, appears to be. The foremost answer to this is, of course, that the people of the country have emphatically pronounced in favour of the same and that it so appears by the last election returns. This, however, is far from conclusive.
Let a policy similar to that presented at the last election, go fairly and squarely before the people; let all the politicians, trusts and manufacturers be honest enough not to mix up things and cloud the issue by screaming treason, waving the flag and appealing to every shade of prejudice, and I am confident that an enormous majority of the people would pronounce in favour of such a policy.
What is this treason of which we hear so much? If any treason exist, it is the conspiracy of the Trusts to compass the ruin of the masses of the people of Canada. Is it really treason of that nature that we hear so much about? I will leave the answer to thbse interested in combines. Where political parties enter into ft fight it should be on a policy; it should be with some higher aim than simply to obtain power, and which ever party follows this doctrine will command more respect in the future.
Kings and Emperors in past centuries had more energy than our much prized ptopular governments have to-day, for as far back as the year 483 of this era, Emperor Zeno, after contemplating the effects of combinations in restraint of trade and loyal competition, had a proclamation issued to the effect that any one found guilty of preventing such loyal competition on food stuffs or other necessaries of life would be condemned to perpetual exile, whilst on the other hand any one guilty of the same offence in respect to articles of luxury was fined. It is plain to see that even in the 5th century there existed conditions and methods similar to those we have at present, and we find it also demonstrable that this Homan Emperor 1,439 years ago made an enormous distinction, by banishing the criminals for ever in the first instance so as to be sure that they would never return to elude the law.
We are not nearly so enlightened today, for the protective policy now in the ascendant seems to favour the very ones
who should be severely punished because their only possible ultimate aim must be the accumulation of millions by the impoverishment of the people at large. Shall we allow this? Another glance at history shows us that similar conditions existed in France prior to 1789 and any one who wants to read history will admit that the effects of those conditions were not strange to the revolution -of that year. It may be said with some appearance of truth that conditions in our country are not nearly so bad as any of those I have alluded to. I am not sure of that. In all _ communities it is considered good policy to cover over running sores and all things not pleasant to look upon, and we all know, at all events, that abuses of any nature are bound to bring about sooner or later the same results.
In an article on industrial and commercial conditions in Germany by Consul-General Frank H. Mason, prepared for the forthcoming ' Volume of Relations of the United States.' Mr. Mason said:
In the report of this series for 1897 the remark was made that as an incident and condition of Germany's perfect organization and industrial growth, its leading productive industries had been syndicated to an extent probably unknown in any other country.
What was true then is still more true to-dav. The two hundred Trusts and Syndicates which are in existence in Germany at the beginning of 1899 are increasing in number day by day, until there is scarcely a single important product of manufacture of which the output, prices and conditions of sale are not governed by a combination or understanding between producers. One can scarcely open a German newspaper without finding a paragraph announcing a new combination of this kind or an article pointing to the recent notable multiplication of^ syndicated industries in England and in the United States as an example of what Germany should do for self protection.
Such is the condition in the great German Empire which on the floor of this House is offered as an example of good administration, and of the benefits of protection.
Speaking on the address in reply to the speech from the Throne at the beginning of the present session, I said, if my memory is correct, that if we kept on looking at Germany until the 12th day of January, we would probably see what the masses thought of this so called model government. Well, the -12th of January has passed, and newspapers have given the results, and some have also commented, but in a very moderate way and why? Because they anticipate in the near future that social conditions in that country may be easily applied to our own.
Oppression of the people by over taxation whether it be by tariff or otherwise,

has the same effect in any civilized country in the world. We may succeed in hampering the movement towards emancipation and freedom for a certain period, but water will find its level and any one who has at heart the wellbeing of his country, and of his fellow men should be in favour of less taxation, less scandalous profits by the mergers and trusts. In any case we no longer live in a time when the people were unorganized masses dependent for their very existence, upon the will of an absolute ruler. Thank God the army of labour is organized and able to defend its rights. The people are awakening to their strength and power and will use it if necessary. They are commencing to understand that protection is a one sided affair as they have no protection for the energy they have to sell:	labour.
What is a Trust? The courts of the United States have, in many cases rendered important decisions on this point. In the. case of Richardson vs. Buhl, the Supreme Court of Michigan said:
All combinations among persons or corporations for the purpose of raising or controlling the prices of merchandise or any of the necessities of life are monopolies and intolerable. and ought to receive condemnation of all courts.
Chief Justice Fuller in delivering the opinion of the Supreme Court in the Sugar case (known as the Knight case) said:
All authorities agreed that in order to vitiate a contract or combination, it is not essential that it shall be a complete monopoly; it is sufficient if it really tends to that end, and to deprive the public of the advantages which follow free competition.
It may be interesting to explain the mode of procedure adopted in the formation of these trusts which are a mere conspiracy to rob the public. We have a good example of these methods in the formation of the Whisky Trust in the United States on July 1, 1898. First of all it is essential to find a promoter whose mission is to carry the operation to a successful end. This promoter must possess two essential qualifications; first, he must be bold and unscrupulous, and second he must have neither conscience nor sense of honour.
To induce a number of industries to amalgamate is sometimes a difficult task; prudence must be exercised. So our promoter will first proceed by persuasion, always exposing the large amount of profits the special industry can realize, and also offering the manufacturer a good price for his co-operation. If he does not succeed he will offer a price far above the value, as is done in almost all cases, and also a special interest in the circulation. If the objections are too great he will spare no promises. If he is unsuccessful he will resort to threats, always arguing that it is Mr. VERVILLE.
of the greatest interest for the manufacturer to join, otherwise the Trust will, be formed without him and he will have then to stand the consequences. If not successful with this method he will employ the last means at his disposal which so far have never failed. War will be declared upon the recalcitrant manufacturer, a commercial war to the death. The Trust will sell to his customers the same goods at lower prices and in seme cases at cost price, knowing full well that they will be in a position to recompense themselves for whatever loss they may have sustained in the operation. They will go so far as to boycott merchants who will buy from that manufacturer. They will refuse him certain patented goods which he cannot purchase elsewhere and cripple him badly. They will then trace a circle around him and the pressure upon him will become so great that he will fall in the clutches of the Trust in a short space of time. An evident proof of this operation has been given by Mr. Clark who fought for a certain time the Whisky Trust in the United States and this is what he said:
I entered the first Trust because I was facin-ated by the gigantic benefits laid before me by the trust, and also by the intolerable persecution to which I was subjected by the organization. I-t was rather against my principles to deprive myself of my liberty. I was then a young man and well able to look after my own business. At last I decided to join and I felt remorse the very same day, although I gathered in great profits for a long time.
What Mr. Clark tells us, many others could corroborate if they dared, but the power of such organization to control the market and even the transportation in many cases prevents them from doing so. Such is the modus operandi in the formation of a trust.
Let us now examine the financial aspect in the formation of Trusts. We may cite as an example the Whisky Trust that Mr. Clark speaks about, and see how easy it is for them to realize dividends on non-existing stock better known as watered stock. On July the first, 1898, was formed the Whisky Trust. The full value of different individual industries absorbed (allowing a margin for overvaluation) was four million dollars. A corporation was then established with an authorized capital of 34 million dollars. 16 millions dollars in common stock and 8 million dollars in preferred stock. Then the following combination intervened.
A financial syndicate was formed in view of facilitating the operation of the Trust. Each of the owners of the absorbed concerns received in kind full value of then individual enterprises, $4,000,000. They received over and above $4,000,000 in com-

mon stock, thus obtaining a net benefit of 100 per cent. In order to receipt itself the financial syndicate received $4,000,000 of preferred stock plus $6,000,000 of common stock, net benefits 150 per cent.
The promoter for his services of very doubtful value to the consumers, received $6,000,000 in common stock. The formation of some of our Trusts in this country must surely be financed in a similar manner. Indeed we have absolute proof that such is the case. While we profess to be afraid of our next-door neighbours, from the commercial standpoint, it would seem that our great financiers are only too willing to copy in every detail their nefarious system of operations in respect Ito the formation of Trusts.
It is said that imitation is the sincerest flattery, but I doubt whether the people at large will appreciate such flattery when it is given at their expense, and at that of their feeling and educating their children.
I will now attempt to make a slight analysis of our good kind of Trusts in Canada, and if possible give some slight idea of the burden that the masses have to bear. I would also desire to suggest some material remedy, of course I cannot expect that my suggestions will immediately appeal to all the members of this House. But such as it is, the remedy I outline appears to me the only one available, and as to its urgency, I think that no one will express any doubt on the subject.
After carefully weighing the significance of the following data, still imperfect although collected at considerable pains, the members of the House will see. I hope that some drastic measures must be taken, not only to prevent the formation of new Trusts, but also to prevent the operation of those now in existence.
The ' Monetary Times ' of January 6th, 1912, published a list of about 40 mergers, giving in one column the capitalization of the merger and in another the canital of the individual companies absorbed, including bonds. The aggregate capitalization of thirty eight of these mergers, according to figures given by the ' Monetary Times,' stands as follows:
Capitalization of mergers .. $336,938,266
Aggregate capital of individual companies absorbed. including bonds .. .. 123,166,588
We can then conclude that the watered stock is .. 213,771,686
The population of Canada being 7,081,869, according to the last census returns, these thirty-eight mergers represent a mortgage of $47.50 on every man, woman and child in the country, or $250 on every family, of which mortgage more than two-thirds represent fictitious or watered stock. What 161
is more important is that every workman's family has to pay about $23 of interest yearly upon the same. This is a heavy tax; yet it does not begin to show the situation of the Canadian public with respeot to Trusts, for it does not include the Ice Trust recently formed, nor the Steel Trust whose capital, according to the 'Monetary Times,' aggregates nearly $100,000,000; nor the Sugar Trusts nor the beef, pork, milk, fruits, cereals, brewing or other food Trusts so detrimental in their present form to the well-being of the people; neither will the Oil Trust be found in the list, nor many of the Trusts on clothing. One that stands prominent is the United Shoe Machinery Company of Canada, with a capitalization of over $45,000,000, and with an annual dividend amounting to $6,117,264, nearly one dollar per head on our population. From all the information to hand, Trusts in Canada as at present constituted already represent an annual average tax of nearly $100 on each family, and this tends constantly to increase.
A glance at the business of the stock exchange of Toronto and Montreal will show this very clearly. McQuaig Bros., of the Montreal Stock Exchange, publish a list of 31 companies and mergers, of which 25 are Canadian, with a total authorized capital of $666,656,975, and a total issue of $932,712,775 which would appear to be beyond the law to the extent of $266,005,300.
Among those will be found the British Columbia Packers' Association, whose net book assets amount to $3,344,871, and whose profits in six years amount to $1,546,422, an average of 20 per cent on their total capital. ,
The Canada Cement merger is of great importance, as cement is being used more and more in building. If there were no merger, it would be more extensively used by workmen in building their own homes. This merger comprises no less than 10 companies, and appears to be capitalized as follows:	Merger capital, $29,000,000;
companies' capital, $17,000,000; watered stock, $12,000,000; net profits of merger (1910), $1,177,698.
The Canadian Locomotive Company is capitalized at $5,000,000. For a few years back their average net profits have been about 5 per cent, after payment of interest on their bonds at 71 per cent, and other charges. This year it is foreseen that their net earnings, after payment of bonds, will be about 18 per cent.
I need not speak of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. We all know what their capital is, and that a large portion of it came originally from government grants, although their earnings aggregate. 17:26 per cent, and they are issuing more stock.

The Canadian Car Foundry Company is capitalized at some $14,000,000. Their profits, after deducting interest on bonds, amounted last year to over 14 per cent.
The Dominion Iron ana Steel Company, and the Dominion Coal Company, who are now clamoring for bounties, are rather a poor-paying concern as mergers go. Just fancy only 4:28 per cent on $35,000,000 of stock, after payment of all interest on bonds and expenses. They, of course, also are issuing new stock. The bounties they are now endeavouring to obtain would mean more than $550,000 annually, and bring their percentage of net profits to about 7 per cent on their present stock. In this connection I wish to state the real labour conditions that exist in the Dominion iron and steel industry, as given by Professor McGill, who made an investigation of them a couple of years ago. In his report he says:
The coke ovens.-These are kept going night and day, the men attending them are mostly foreigners-228 come from Europe, 15 from the United Kingdom, 61 from Newfoundland, and 58 are Canadians. Most of the work is such that Canadians do not apply for it. They are divided into shifts. Taking the total, 272 work ten hours and 63 work twelve hours per shift.
The coke ovens have been greatly extended since this report. I am told that 800 men are employed in this department, 90 per cent of whom are foreigners and1 receive $1.40 per day. Continuous operation, 7 days per week, 365 days in the year.
Open hearth furnaces.-These are kept going night and day. and the men attending them work in two shifts. Taking the totals of the shifts, 306 men work twelve hours each, 7 work eleven hours, and 82 work ten hours. Of the total force about 36 per cent are Canadians. 29 per cent are Europeans, 19 per cent are Newfoundlanders, 8 per cent are British, and the remainder are Americans or West Indians.
In his department I am told the force employed is about 600. Melters, about 20, receive from $4.50 to $5 per day, and helpers $2.50, third helpers, $1.80, general labourers $1.40, the latter class constituting the majority.
The blast furnaces.-These also operate continuously, and the men are divided into two shifts. Taking the totals, 226 work twelve hours, 13 work eleven hours, and 64 work ten hours.
In this department blowers and heaters get $3.50 per day, second helpers $2.50, third helpers $1.80, and about 120 general labourers $1.40.
The mills.-There are about 430 men at work in the blooming, rail and rod mills. Of these, over 350 work in twelve-hour shifts, and the remainder work ten hours. The day Mr. VERVILLE.
force is larger than the night force. About fifty per cent of the men are Canadians, and about twenty-four per cent are from Newfoundland, so that the percentage of European labour is small. The mills _ are kept going continuously. There is some time lost.
In this department the pay is about the same as the above. There are a few well-paid rollers and heaters, but the majority receive a bare existence, or, to be concise, 14 cents per hour. A new feature has been introduced in the shape of a staff beginning work at nine o'clock Sunday evening, truly a remarkable state of things in a Christian country.
Speaking of the Transportation Department, the professor says:
There are about sixty-four men engaged at the piers loading and unloading vessels. This work lasts only during the summer months. The men are employed only during the summer, differing in this respect from the dock and wharf labourers in Halifax. When there are no vessels at the piers, the men are paid time wages, and the work is cleaning, &c. When the vessels are in, they work two twelve hour shifts, and aTe paid tonnage rates. It w'ould be impossible for them to do as much in eight hours as in twelve. An eight hour law would mean the employment of three eight hour shifts. This would mean an increase in the force, and if the system and rates of wages remained the same, a decrease in individual earnings. The work, while the vessels are in, is steady, hut when there are no ships in, it is light.
There are from 80 to 100 men running the engines, &c., on the company's tracks. These work in two twelve hour shifts.
Regarding work on the pieTS, it is true the work is seasonal, it is worse, cases have been known of men working 48 hours continuously in loading the vessels.
In the case of the locomotive men, please note that it calls for seven days per week with a 24 hour shift every two weeks.
Yards.-(350 men at $1.40 per day). In the yards, and stables about 200 men are employed. A few of those work twelve hours, and the majority ten per day. Much of the work requires no skill, and a considerable percentage of the labour is foreign. An eight hour day would lead to the employment of a larger number of men, but it is impossible to say what increase would be Deoessary.
Other Employees.-There are about two dozen gateman, watchmen and janitors, and about the same number of timekeepers and scalemen. All these ' work ' twelve hours. An eight hour law would necessarily mean three eight hour shifts.
I am informed that the general labourers in the yards are ordered out on- Sundays, on the one hand necessity is the whip and failure to turn out means the * sack.'
The other employees not mentioned are the innovation of General Manager Rutter, to wit:	The spies and blue coated
gentlemen under the charge of one Noble by name, but otherwise by occupation.

The employees have asked for an investigation by the Labour Department about two years ago, on the grounds that the fair wages resolution applied to the steel company, as receiving grants from public funds. They claim that the company were not paying current wages in the case of bricklayers, carpenters and others as labourers. Mr. Dubreuil, fair wages officer of the Labour Department, -went to investigate; he sought an interview with General Manager Butler, who politely told him and the government he represented that they could go to a warmer tolace than in the tovens of the company, that they would not stand for any interference with their business.
The report continued:
Foreign Labour.-A little over 40 per cent of the employees are Canadians, 28 per cent are from the continent of Europe, 20 per cent are from Newfoundland, 7 per cent from the United Kingdom, and the remainder from the United States and the West Indies. The European labour comes mainly from Poland, Hungary, Italy and France, though almost every European nation is represented. The European labour is found chiefly in the yards, coke ovens and among the helpers at the open hearth furnaces. The Newfoundland labour is found also in these departments, and to a greater extent at the blast furnaces and in the mills. All told nearly 60 per cent of the labour is imported.
Wages.-The majority of the men are paid by the hour. A system of payment by tonnage or bonus has been introduced and is being extended. Between 500 and 600 men were affected by this system during the year 1908.
An anaylsi9 of the labour cost taken from their own figures of 1908 as being 2.03 which includes superintendence, will show the $1.40 men to be the major portion of the employees of this corporation.
The Mechanical Department.-About 400 .men are engaged in this department. Of these 70 work twelve, and the remainder ten hours per shift, the day shift being much larger than the night shift. About 70 per cent of these men are Canadians, and nearly all the others are from Newfoundland and the United Kingdom. The men are machinists, foundry men, boiler makers, blacksmiths, pipe fitters, carpenters, pattern makers, &c.
' Regarding the machinists, half of the staff are ordered out each Sunday.
Another incident worth noticing is the percentage of Canadians, which is dwindling, their places being taken by ' British born.'

The policy of the company is to pay perhaps half a dozen in each department the maximum, the remainder having the incentive bf the higher pay to lure them into all the pathways of envy, hatred, and uncharitableness. That is how they keep men divided.
The Nova ScQtia Steel and Coal Company, however, has done better than this. The percentage earned on common stock, in 1910, was 10.97 per cent, and if they ever received bounties, this company will be placed on a really handsome basis as to prbfits.
The Dominion Textile Company, who have been clamouring that it was impossible to pay reasonable wages to men, women and children in their employ, and have tried to convince the Department of Labour that their employers had to submit for the present at least to starvation wages, are capitalized at about $14,000,000, and after payment of all charges the company nets annually some $990,000 to be divided amongst the shareholders, leaving besides a substantial surplus. Last year the holders of their preferred stock received the equivalent of 22.4 per cent on their holdings. In the last few days this company have had remorse and have decided to increase the wages of those ptoor people who have been clamouring for an increase for so long. I suppose -when they are in a position to pay 22 per cent on their stock, which will probably run to 35 per cent tor 40 per cent, they feel that they can give a slice of their vast earnings to those who have placed them in a position to earn that money.
The Montreal Cotton Company, Limited, on the other hand, with a capital of about $7,000,000, only shows an average earning *of about 10 per cent on all stock.

Is the hon. gentleman sure bf his figures as to the capitalization, when he says $12,000,000 and some odd hundred thousands? I can tell the hon. gentleman that he is positively wrong.
My hon friend will have to blame the official journal from which I have taken the figures. I have taken from the ' Monetary Times.'
As an officer of that company, I may tell the hon. gentleman that the capital is $2,200,000 preferred stock, and the same amount of common. I am glad to correct him in his figures.

As I have already said,
I am always citing from the 'Monetary Times', which is an official journal, and which has a pretty good standing. Of course I am willing to accept any correction the hon. gentleman may make; but at the same time it would be proper to have the correction made in the 'Monetary Times' likewise, which is a journal scattered over the country. Now if we are well informed a great many of these small institutions have since the formation of the Trust been closed, the consideration of small towns or villages has had no consideration, the consumers have felt to a large extent the formation of the Trust also the producer who has now only one buyer. The Trust I am informed goes further by setting the retail price to the corner grocery store. Here I wish to cite some paragraphs of the agreement which I have taken from the ' Grain Growers' Guide,' not a bad authority. William Miller Collier, in his book on Trusts, tells us some of the effects of the Trusts on wages, and this is what he says :
The effects of excessive capitalization, and the attempt to pay dividends upon such capitalization, are a tendency to create artificial earnings upon an artificial capital both by artificially raising the price of the article produced, and by the depreciation of the wages paid. The result to the public from an economical standpoint is objectionable.
The question has more than once been asked: What remedy should be applied to such a state of things, and what action,
legislative or otherwise, can be devised in order to prevent this undue development of mergers, every time the answer has been legislation. In my opinion this is a mistake, we have too much legislation on the statute-books at present, and it would take up all the time at the disposal of our courts of justice to enforce the laws already made. Let me mention them:
1.	By the British Wages Act, section 91, subsection 2, in the parliament of Canada is vested of legislation in matter of trade and commerce.
2.	The Trade Union Act of 1872, reenacting in substance the British Trade Union Act of 1872, forecasts legislation against combinations in restraint of trade by exempting before hand trade unions from the operation of any such laws. Embodied in the Eevised Statutes.
3.	In 1889, subsequent to the findings of the committee of the House of Commons and of the Labour Commission of 1888, parliament enacts a law for the suppression of combinations in restraint of trade. Embodied in the Criminal Code, sections 496-498 (Revised Statutes, 1906).
4.	The usefulness of the above provisions was materially increased by parliament in 1900, by an amendment omitting the word ' unlawful ' in the definition of a conspiracy in restraint of trade, thus shifting the burden of protof upon the accused.
5.	In 1895, and again in 1898, the Hon. Dr. Sproule introduced Bills to regulate Trusts, but they are not carried through.
6.	The Customs Tariff Act of 1897, section 18, provides that when it shall be established that there exists any trust or combination with regard to any article of commerce, the Governor in Council shall place such article upon the free list, or so reduce the duty as to give the public the benefit of reasonable competition.
7.	By an amendment to the Inland Revenue Act (chapter 17, 1904) the minister is empowered to cancel the manufacturing license of any company selling goods under restrictive conditions.
8.	Parliament adopted in 1910, 9 and 10 Edward VII, chapter 9, an Act to provide for the investigation of combines, monopolies, trusts and mergers, the object of which is to make the ouerati'on of such concerns public through the action of the courts.

At present we have a system of_ cold storage in the country, which, from its origin, has done more harm than good. At its inception, the cold storage system was built up and subsidized from a humanitarian standpoint, but the invention has been abused, and the cold storage warehouses have furnished the means to overtax our population and to starve them to a certain extent. If it were possible to obtain the number of pounds of food stuffs in cold storage warehouses, the price paid for merchandise stor ed in the months of November, December and January, and also the retail price paid by the consumers, we would understand the enormous profits made by these institutions.
We are told that millions of pounds of butter and cheese are now in storage in our large cities. Butter that was bought for 24 cents per pound is now being sold for 45 cents. Eggs are being imported, though there is a good quantity now in storage, and they -were sold lately for 50 cents a dozen, and they were far from being fresh. Before leaving for downstairs he adjusts his 10 per cent artificial teeth, and then descends to light a fire in a 25 per cent stove with 25 per cent charcoal, which he carries in a 25 per cent pail. He then sits down on a 30 per cent chair at a 30 rer cent table covered with a 30 per cent table cloth, his knees being protected by a 30 per cent table napkin. These things arranged, he daily takes his 30 per cent tool bag filled with 30 per cent nails, 30 per cent tools, .25 per cent axe, carries a 30 per cent crowbar, lights his 35 per cent pipe with his 50 cents a pound tobacco, fixes his 30 per cent hat firmly on his head and hustles off through the dark of the morning guided by the light from 30 per cent gas lamps. His wife smiles at him through a 15 per cent window, probably thinking of the new 30 per cent bonnet which she has purchased and glad of the fact that her day, too, is over, with freedom from 35 per cent clothes wringers, 35 per cent curtains, 20 per cent brooms, 25 per cent brushes, 35 per cent baby carriages. This statement may seem ridiculous, but nevertheless it exposes clearly the well protected workman.

Statesmen of to-day should read the prophetic words written by the great American statesman, Abraham Lincoln, in 1865:
I see in the near future a crisis approaching that enerves me and causes me to tremble for the safety of my country.
As a result of the war corporations have been enthroned and an era of corruption in high places will follow and the money power of the country will endeavour to prolong its reign upon the prejudices of the people until all the wealth is aggregated into a few hands and the republic is destroyed. He gives us to understand that this condition of things has been brought about since September 21 last. But you did not find fault with them in all that time. I do not think much of the men who stand on the doorstep of Cobden and shout free trade principles to the present generation. 1 think a tariff of 26 per cent on an average is a protective tariff, that it has_ the principle of protection as much imbedded in it as any tariff we have ever had in this country. Canada and1 that it will be secure, and not at the caprice of any sect of men. I do not pretend to say that it is a wise thing for any public man to arouse a suspicion against any class of people; on the contrary it is a misfortune. The callings of peo/ple in this country are largely a matter of their own selection. A man chooses to be an agriculturist, or a merchant, or a mechanic, or a professional man, and the door is open to him, he can reach the position he desires, no matter what his birth may be. It is largely a matter of choice. But when be makes his choice, it is not right for him to question the sincerity of another man who makes a different choice; they follow different lines to success. Now I do not follow with prejudice or hatred the man who leaves the log-house and makes his way up through the battle of life to _a palace. I follow that man with pride in his success.	_
There are problems before this country; hon. gentleman opposite have left many problems unsolved that they have at least attempted to solve in the interest of the people. These problems to-day are at the threshold of the Conservative party; and I hope that party will have the genius, the sincerity and the ability to deal with these problems and solve them in the interest of the people of Canada. Why should this country, a great agricultural country, after fifteen years of Liberal rule, and with a practical farmer as Minister of Agriculture, be importing four or five of the most important agricultural products for table use? that confront him? I say, no. While the artisans and people generally will be more cheaply fed, the farmer will be better off. That is the solution of this problem,	but it is

tleman into that county. He came here with six or eight children, he had about $1,200 to the good after paying expenses. Surely it is in the interest of this whole country that that should be done. Many of our people are going west. You cannot proscribe any one of our people from going west. Now, we must, in order to maintain our social conditions, our schools, our churches, and all those things that pertain to a good neighbourhood, we must do something to maintain them in their strength, and in their usefulness, and to my mind1 that is a solution of many of the difficulties that we have just heard mentioned.
But what has been done by hon. gentlemen opposite to bring to the notice of that class of people in Europe the older provinces of this Dominion, within the last ten years? For my part, I hope the present government will take up those matters and solve them along these practical lines, upon which they can be solved1. Take up a list of the people that are going out of the older provinces into our western country-and it is a good thing to have

We find this agr.cultural country, with all its splendid possibilities, buying its butter, its meat, its eggs, and some other produce from other countries. I can't understand it. market and go where they are exporting grain now. I cannot understand it. For every bushel you send into the American west, you have to send a bushel out of Boston or New York. The conditions are abnormal, and these conditions will be best solved, not by fanning the discontent, but by showing that you are making an honest effort to remove the difficulties. My hon. friend (Mr. Verville) thinks that this surplus should be expended in lessening taxation. Well, there is another legacy that has been left us by hon. gentlemen opposite, the enormous expenditure on the Transcontinental railway, an expenditure double or treble their own estimate. We are proposing to meet these responsibilities that are thrown upon us, I say largely by mismanagement, if not by mismanagement, then by miscalculation. men governing this country should have launched out into an undertaking of that magnitude without, knowing more about it. I do not say that we should have a high tariff in this country, but I venture to say that, while it may not be much higher than hon. gentlemen left it, it will be more consistently adjusted and will not be hugger-mugger until you do not know where the tariff is. There is nothing in heaven above or in earth beneath like it. There is nothing in any country in the world like the tariff which these hon. gentlemen left on the statute-books. They have a preference, a maximum, a minimum, and dear knows what. They go to the farmer and they say: We have lowered the duty on carriages; under the British preference the duty is lowered on carriages from England. But, it was raised on carriages coming from the United States and that is where people buy their carriages. They fixed the tariff so that they could go to this man and say: We have lowered the tariff, and so that they could go to the other man and say:	We have raised the
tariff. They could go to the carriage maker in Ontario and say:	We have raised the
tariff, and they could go to the man using a carriage and say: We have lowered the tariff. How many mowing machines or carriages do we buy in England? The articles on which the duty has been lowered under the British preference to the farmer are the articles that he does not get from Great Britain at all. He gets them from the United States against which you have raised the tariff barrier. You claim that you have lowered the tariff under the British preference. That is scarcely fair-play to the innocent man, yet, that is the fact. I say that the tariff in this country should be a tariff that would be understood. It requires an expert every day in the year, except Sunday, and he has Mr. BRODER.
to think of it then if he is honest in his endeavour to act in the public interest, to tell what the tariff means as applied to different goods that are coming into this country. He has got to sit up nights in order to apply it, and then he makes mistakes. That is the tariff that has been left on the statute-book by the free traders who have gone out of power. They are getting back to the old platform. The_ right hon. leader of the opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laur-ier) said away back in 1893 when they were making their platform, that he did not intend to skin the bear till he killed it. Oh, no, he killed the bear but he never skinned it. It is there with its skin on as much as it ever was.
That is a skin game.
Yes, he said that in that 1893 convention right here in this town. Yet, these hon. gentlemen opposite did not do what they promised. It was free trade that they promised then.
Blue ruin is their platform now.

We are in power to-day and they are driven back in desperation to the idols of old. I do not blame them for that. This recalls to my mind a story, and it is a lawyer's story, that I am going to tell to these free traders across the way. There was a man in Ireland who wandered into a grave-yard to amuse himself. You can amuse yourself in a grave-yard in Ireland. He came to a grave-stone on which was the inscription: Sacred to the memory of Mr. So-and-So, an eminent lawyer and a Christian. He said:	This is a strange
country; I see they bury two men in one grave. That is the kind of graves we will have all over this country when these men die. They will be putting two men in one grave. I do not see how you could bury them in any other way, because you will have to bury the free trader and protectionist in one grave. They were all buried on the 21st of September, and all we have to do now is to put the inscription on the tombstone. I am suggesting that we will have to bury two men in one grave. Leave well enough alone.
Yes, we are going to continue as we are. Do you want things left as they are? Do you want the principle of protection to be continued in the tariff?
I said: Leave well enough alone.

I want to know if you want the tariff left as it is to-day. If the Iron, gentleman said that he did, for the next ten years he could not say a word.

They do not want to leave things as they are. They expect them to be improved and they will not be disappointed. The people 'of this country expect practical, common sense in the government. They do not want a lot of rhetoric; they want something that is tangible, and they want an improvement in the present conditions. I believe that they can be improved and that the government who are in power to-day have opportunities that perhaps no government that ever came into power, in this great country, with its possibilities, have had. The public men of the country must use the common sense they have, get down close to the people and help them solve those serious problems which must be solved not only in the interest of the country at the present time, but with a view to its future welfare.

I was struck by some of the remarks made by the Minister of Finance yesterday, and they were in line with utterances of the Premier and the Minister of Trade and Commerce, made in the early part of the session. He spoke of the bounties of Providence, the success and development of this country due to ils natural advantages and to the energy of its people. The inference which I think he desired to convey, and which the Premier and the Minister of Trade and Commerce certainly desired to convey, was that the administra-162i
tion and policy of the late government had practically nothing to do with the desirable financial conditions that prevail in the country at the present time, when its revenues are higher than ever before, when it has a greater surplus than has ever before existed, when immigrants are coming in greater volume than ever before, when its prosperity is increasing at a greater ratio than ever before. I have heard the Minister of Trade and Commerce in previous sessions make the same suggestion from this side of the House. Now, there cannot be success without the foundations of success. A country cannot succeed and be prosperous unless it has the material means whereby success may be achieved. But if a country, no n atter how advantageously situated, can succeed without capable and competent direction, then a country is the only institution or organization in the known wond that can succeed on these terms.
Inasmuch as the government of a country is the most complex piece of machinery that exists in connection with any human enterprise, I submit that in the very nature of things the policy of the government must to a stupendous degree be given credit or blame for the result that is achieved in the well-being of that country. I say this not because I wish to claim any credit on behalf of the late government, but to point out to the friends of the present government and to the people of Canada that if our friends undertake to conduct the government of this country on the principle that it does not make very much difference to the welfare or prosperity of the country whether the government has a forward or * a backward policy, whether it has a developing or a restrictive policy, they will find, and the country will find, that they have made a great mistake. The policy of a government, in the nature of things, must have a great effect upon the well-being of the country, and if our friends have not yet realized that fact then I hope they soon will realize it, because we are all anxious to see development and progress in Canada.
If it is thought that the progress and prosperity that has been achieved has come simply because the sun has shone and the soil is fertile, and our people are energetic and industrious, I would ask, was it the fertile soil or the industry of the people, or the act of Providence, or the shining of the sun that entered upon the undertaking of the National Transcontinental Railway? Was it Providence that deepened the canals? Is it Providence that is building the port of Montreal? Is it not the aggressive-and intelligent action of a progressive government having a progressive policy that has absolutely and directly brought into being this condition of affairs?

A word with regard to this eastern section of the National Tarnscontinental railway. My hon. friend from Dundas (Mr. Broder), as his friends have always done, decried the building of that section of the railway, and yet the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce on former occasions in this House tried to discredit the late government because that railway was not completed before to-day. Did you ever hear of men taking such an attitude? These gentlemen exhausted every effort that could he put forth to prevent the construction of that great public enterprise, and when they could not prevent its construction, no later than some two or tlhree weeks ago in this House, on their responsibility as ministers of the Crown, they attempted to discredit it as a profitable enterprise, after attacking the government because it was not completed more quickly.
I said that the government was not changing the tariff. They are entitled to credit for that, and I am sure that this country breathed a sigh of relief when the announcement was made yesterday that there would be neither changes in the tariff nor the establishment of bounties. We really got off better than we exipected, but we were not less gratified to hear tlhat the policy of constructive development which had been entered upon iby the late government, and which had been carried so far towards completion, is to be still continued by our 'friends on the other side of the House. The two Transcontinental railways and the Hudson Bay railway are all to be completed, and the ports are to be equipped. All that the late government undertook to do or had in progress of doing is to be carried on without change by our friends the new government. For this again the country is thankful.

House resumed at eight o'clock.

Shortly before the House rose at six o'clock, I had alluded to the fact that the budget recently presented to the House offered no variation from the tariff prevailing when the late government went out of power. That, however, is hardly a complete statement of the situation. The position of the late government in regard to tariffs is set out, not in the schedules on the statute-book, but in the proposition placed before the country, generally known as the reciprocity arrangement, This arrangement was the policy of the late government in regard to tariff readjustment, and was their policy also in dealing with the questions that were then up for immediate consid-Mr. OLIVER.
eration in the interest of the people. The tariff as represented in the reciprocity arrangement involved a policy of reduction of taxation and expansion of trade. The reduction of taxation was the means taken by the late government to deal with the question of combines, the question of the high cost of living and also the question of the readjustment of the burden of taxation. It is futile to say that the late government did not move as it should have movecl in the direction of lower tariffs. The tariff as it was proposed under the reciprocity arrangement was especially a reduction in regard to food products; it was essentially aimed at the high cost of living. It was believed that by taking the duty entirely off the more important food .stuffs and reducing the duty in regard to practically all others, the cost of living to the people of Canada would be reduced. This could not be done without, in some degree and to some extent, affecting the profits of the combines and mergers which had been formed during the preceding years. And, as soon as it was announced that the policy of the government was to reduce the cost of the food of the people, at once these combines, trusts and mergers, whose organization was entered upon for the express purpose of levying an unjust toll upon the food of the people, rallied in antagonism to the late government and its policy. And the result of that rally is the success of our hon. friends on the other side. It has been said frequently that the late government was not true to low tariff principles because for so many years of its term in office no serious reductions had been made in the tariff. Let me point out that, situated as we are alongside of the United States, the half of our total trade being done with the United States and that country being a food-producing country like our own, if at any time during their fifteen years of power the late government had removed the duty on food stuffs, those who to-day criticise, and on all previous occasions have criticised, the late government because it 'did not move more rapidly towards reductions of the tariff, would have been the loudest in their declarations against its attitude and action. It was not practicable, in the ordinary sense of the word, for Canada to abolish the duty on foodstuffs unless our neighbours on the other side of the line did the same. But, when the government of the United States saw fit to reverse the policy it had followed for forty years of maintaining a high tariff on foodstuffs, the Liberal government, the government of low tariffs and fair-play to the individual citizen, did not lose one moment in closing with the proposition and staking its existence as a government upon the acceptance of the proposition by the

people. Whatever allegations may be made against the late government, the allegation of bad faith toward the principle of low tariff can never, in fairness, be made in view of their record on that occasion. It is a surprising fact that, in face of the high cost of living prevailing in Canada and of the complaints that have continually been made in regard to that condition, such a proposition did not receive the approval of the majority of the electors. That it did not receive their approval is only another tribute to the strength, and vigour the energy, and, may I venture to say, the unscrupulousness, of those interests that, on the sound of alarm on the declaration that the government was for lowering the tariff, rallied their forces in opposition, stopping at no consideration of honesty or fair-play, or loyalty to either Canada or the empire, in order to secure the defeat of the government.

So far as my information goes, the facts are

Yes, and I will tell you why. Eight years ago we paid the farmer $20 a ton for peas, to-day we are offering him $34 a ton for peas. Eight years ago we paid him 18 cents for tomatoes, to-day we are paying him 30 cents. Eight years ago we paid him $5 a ton for corn, to-day we are paying him $8.

speechtext:
It seems to me that the hon. member -who has the floor ought to be allowed courteously to continue his speech and that such unseemly interruptions are not becoming to the dignity of the House of Commons or in keeping with fair debate.
Mr. OLIVER, The United States tariff is 2 1-2 cents to 40 per cent, and the rate-

now proposed for both the United States and Canada is a cent and a quarter. The reduction by the United States is 1-1 to 2 cents per pound and the reduction by Canada a quarter of a cent. I' think i have established the point that the reciprocity arrangement, the proposal to reduce the duties on food products in Canada and thereby reduce the cost of living, did not necessarily affect to the extent of that reduction the price received by the farmer when there was a combine standing between the producer and the consumer and that in so far as the reciprocity arrangement brought competition into the distribution of such food products, to that extent, the consumer gained and the producer did not lose. I have been delayed somewhat in the course of my argument by the question-the very proper question - of the hon. member for Peterborough and I hope that I will be excused for now continuing.
I say that it was absolutely established-as the policy of the late government to reduce the cost of living by reducing the taxation on food products and that that policy was entered upon at the very first moment when it could reasonably be entered upon and expect the endorsation of the people, all things being considered. Just as soon as it became possible for Canada to secure entry to the United States market for food products on fair terms, just at that moment, the government of Canada was prepared to make corresponding reductions in the tariff on such products coming into Canada and thereby benefit the consumers and reduce the cost of living to the people of Canada. The late government undertook to answer the question as to what should be done in regard to the high cost of living and in regard to the exactions of combines. The country is interested in knowing what they may expect at the hands of the present government in regard to the same matters. It -is to be regretted that since the present government came into power the cost of living has not decreased. It has increased. The formation of combines has not ceased. There have been more rather than less.
The country is interested in knowing what attitude this government will take now that it is in power, in regard to these pressing and important matters. Whatever the late government may have been or dene is not the question to-day, although the late government is quite prepared to stand on its record. But the question is: What is this government going to do; and we can judge of what it is going to do by what it has done. I took the liberty of suggesting earlier in the discussion that the present government, when it comes tc frame a tariff, will frame that tariff in the inter-Mr. OLIVER.
ests of the combines, not in the interest of l educing the cost of living, not in the interest of reducing taxation. I say that if the government is true to the policy and the principles upon which it attained office, it will be a government of increased taxation and restricted trade. And, Mr. Speaker, in my humble judgment, such a policy cannot tend to the well-being, or the-progress, or the prosperity of this country. We have had some experience of the actions of this government, although they have not introduced changes in the tariff. They have been in power for five months, and in a country like this a great deal happens in five months. I submit that it is no answer for their failure to deal in the public interest with great questions as th^y arise, to say that they have not been long in office. It is not necessary to tell us that. They have been so busy removing officials appointed by the late government, so busy appointing commissions to find places for their friends, in parliament and out of parliament, that they have not had time to pay attention to those matters of first importance in which all the people of the whole country are interested. There have been matters brought to the attention of this government, not only by those -on this side of the House, but by their own friends as well. The member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) has taken the country into his confidence-I do not know whether he has taken the government into his confidence or not-he has told the country that there is a condition of affairs west of Lake Superior that demands the instant and urgent attention of the government. I think my hon. friend the member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) is imbued with the same idea, so-that if our friends opposite are not aware of the existing conditions, and if they have-not taken any action in regard to these conditions, it is not for lack of knowledge. I submit it is not for lack of time, because, if they were spending their time in that which was of greater importance to the country and not in that which was of greater importance ro their party and their friends, they would have had plenty of time. It has been said in the House, it has been repeated in the press, and it is well known throughout all Canada to-day, that to that part of Canada which chiefly produces food products for export, access to the markets of the United States was an important feature of the then government's proposal last spring. Insome parts of the country access to the producing areas of the United States so as to reduce the cost of living was desirable; in -other parts of the country access to the -consuming markets of the United States was desirable in order to secure greater benefit to our people. Our friends in the government are proposing to extend Can-

ada's trade by a treaty with the West Indies, and I think I have read in some place that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is going to visit Australia with a view to our increasing our trade with that country. But, there are the trade possibilities which were open to Canada by the lowering of the duty on food products going into the United States, an opportunity which would add to the value of every bushel of the farmers' products in all the three prairie provinces. That proposal was as available to this government as it was to the late government, and if to-dav the farmers of the western prairies are selling their wheat at an average of ten cents a bushel less than they could -have obtained for it, the fault lies not with the late government but with this government, and to this government the loss must be charged. It is true that this is not in line with the policy of trade restriction upon which the government were elected, and I think it cannot be emphasized too strongly in the minds of the people, just exactly what loss is being suffered by reason of that restrictive policy.

If we had. say for purposes of illustration, a dozen transcontinental lines, so that there would be no congestion of traffic, would the hon. gentleman not then say that that was quite equal to wha.t be proposes in the way of a reciprocal market?

Not at all The suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Burnham) does not touch the point. I will deal with the point he has raised later on. But for the moment I am dealing simnly with the question of the advantage to the western producer of access to the markets of the United States for his products, and I say that the market reports show that the advantage in the United States markets on the 2nd of March averages about ten cents a bushel on wheat, fourteen cents a bushel on white oats, and from twenty-four to sixty-four cents a bushel on barley.
Is it not a fact that the price of wheat was higher in Manitoba on the 20th of September last, the day before the election, than it was in North Dakota?

I do not know, and I do not know what difference that makes. The question is, what is the price of wheat now and what has it been ever since? If my hon. friend is going to put before this country the idea that because his friends have been returned to power the price of wheat in Canada has gone down, he is welcome to that contention; but I would think he would be the last man to make such a proposition, and I want him to be my witness that I have not made that suggestion.

The hon. gentleman knows as well as any man in this House that a premium is paid for hard wheat in North Dakota at the present time. He knows that the millers at Minneapolis thought that reciprocity was going to carry in Canada, and for that reason the price of hard wheat went down in North Dakota, and the price in Manitoba on the 20th of September last was higher than in North Dakota, showing conclusively that reciprocity would have been no good for western Canada.	-

The only flaw in my hon. friend's argument is that the difference in price is greater on damaged wheat than it is on sound wheat, greater on soft wheat than on hard wheat, greater on barley than on wheat, greater on flax than on wheat and greater on oats than on wheat. So that my hon. friend has no ground whatever for his suggestion unless he contends that because of the return of this government to power the price of wheat in Canada has gone down.
I never said that. I said that the price In North Dakota went down. I did not say the price in Canada went down.
The price in North Dakota to-day is an average of ten cents a bushel higher than in Manitoba. Therefore the price in North Dakota must have gone up, or the price in Manitoba must have gone down.	.
[DOT] Does the hon. gentleman as a western representative think that we would get the prices quoted in the United States to-day if we had reciprocity with the United States?

There comes to my mind the case of a rich man who was dying and whose pastor suggested that he might leave his money to the church. The dying man wanted to know what effect that would be likely to have upon his future condition. The minister said that he could not tell, but suggested that there would be no harm in trying. There would be no harm in our trying the effect of access to a market where the price has been persistently for four months ten cents a bushel higher than it has been on our market, and has been persistently year after year in that condition. Not every day, I will admit; but as a rule the Dakota price has been better than the Manitoba price, and my hon. friend is my authority for this statement, in a speech which he delivered in this House in 1909.
Would that condition continue under reciprocity?

My opinion is: yes, undoubtedly. But it is not a question of opinion; it is a question of fact. I say that, with a population of ninety millions of people consuming wheat, and wanting the best, there is a sufficient demand in the United States for our special quality of wheat to keep the price at a premium for home consumption in the United States. That is my belief, and I think nobody will contradict it.
They wanted it for export.

They are not exporting a bushel of that kind of wheat, and if my hon. friend does not know it, my hon. friend behind him (Mr. Sharpe, Lisgar) will tell him. I think I have established thoroughly that the policy of this government has cost the prairie country, on a fair estimate, not less than $12,000,000 during the current year. Is that a loss only to the prairie country? Is not that a loss that will affect every interest in Canada, and particularly the manufacturing interests of eastern Canada?
Do I understand you to say that they offered reciprocal trade without a quid pro quo?

They offered it for a
consideration.
How do you claim, then, that it would be a benefit to the whole of Canada?
I am saying that the loss of $12,000,000 of newly-created wealth to the western farmer is a loss to the whole Dominion of Canada. I hope my hon. friend understands that.
I do not.

Then I am sorry. There has been a great deal of talk about a division between the east and the west. Let me say that the eastern manufacturer is directly interested in the loss of that amount of money to the western farmer -that the eastern commercial house, the eastern financial interest, every interest, even the canners' combine, is interested.
What about the eastern farmer, who turned your party ou|t of office?

That is his privilege. I am not arguing with my hon. friend on that point at all. May I be allowed to continue my address, unless my hon. friend has some light to throw on the subject? I want to emphasize the point that every interest in eastern Canada is interested in the western farmer and in his getting every cent of value that can be got for his crop; and when the eastern manufacturer lined up his men before

.
the 21st of September and told them that if reciprocity carried1, the factory would have to be shut up and they would be out of employment, he told them what was not the fact. He urged them to vote against what was in their best interest and in his best interest, as well as in the best interest of this country as a whole.
How about the member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie)?

The member for South Wellington can answer for himself, and I think he is quite competent to answer any of my friends on the other side of the House who may wish to ask him any questions. I have estimated the loss to the western farmer and to all Canada by reason of failure to secure access to the United States markets for the western products at $12,000,000 in this current year. But our hon. friends will say that it is contrary to their policy to allow the western farmer to sell his products on the other side of the line. I think mv hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. White) suggested that we ought to build up a milling industry in Canada and bund up our railway system by defeating reciprocity. That is to say while we have a tariff that compels the producer to buy in a protected market we are also going to reject an arrangement that would enable him to sell otherwise than in a restricted market.
But there is another condition in the country in regard to which relief might be given in a manner less directly contrary to the policy of our government, I speak of the condition of traffic congestion or grain blockade. That matter has been brought to the attention of the House and the government have given their answer in regard to it, they have told us we must not complain of the dispensations of Providence, that they have not been in office very long and have been very busy, they have had something else to do than to take care of the conditions as they exist. Let me emphasize those conditions. It has been stated here and elsewhere that by reason of the lower prices resulting from the grain blockade the western farmer loses on this year's operations not less than $10,000,000, and he stands to lose $6,000,000 more by reason of the total destruction of damaged grain. That is to say he stands to lose $16,000,000 as a result of the inadequacy of the transportation facilities in that country in regard to this year's crop. But our friends say that this is a condition that cannot be avoided. They say that in one breath and in the next breath they say: We have taken measures to avoid it. They have succeeded in making arrangements with the railway companies so that this grain can be delivered bv a short haul to St. Paul and Duluth instead of being taken

to St. John-and if they had made those arrangements so that they would have ccme into effect on November 10 instead of on March 7, there would not have been any grain blockage, there would not have been any loss to the farmer either in depressed prices or in loss of damaged grain. This government has been convicted by its own action of having stood silent and quiet and careless wline this country has lost $10,000,000 and stands to lose $6,000,000 more when it need not have lost one cent had an aggressive and energetic government, one that was paying attention to the needs of the country, been in office. If they take refuge in the statement that their policy is averse to sending Canada's trade across the line, then I ask, why did they make arrangements to have it go south of the line? If they say it is not contrary to their policy then they stand convicted of having lost to the western farmer and to this country the stupendous sum of from $10,000,000 to $16,000,000 without the slightest justification on earth. There are times when a policy may very well be abandoned.
Hear, hear.

There are times when a policy may very well be abandoned, and this was certainly one of those times. Yet when I had the honour to place before the House a resolution approving of the action of the government, desiring to confirm them in the policy which they ultimately adapted, they rejected the resolution, and their followers voted against it to a man, declared absolutely against a policy that would have relieved' the situation of this year; and in all human probability such action will be just or almost as necessary next year. We have on record the votes of the members of the government and their followers in the House declaring absolutely against the very policy that they themselves were compelled to undertake, only at too late a date in this year. I do not know just how far the excuse of lack of time should prevail. When a government is charged with the responsibility of office, when they have assumed with all readiness that responsibility, I am not sure just how far lack of time is an excuse for lack of action.
Another matter that has been discussed in the west for some time and brought to the attention of this House by formal resolution, is the question of the equalization of local railway rates. Surely there could be nothing more fair, more reasonable, more right than that the railway! companies should not be allowed to charge more on the western prairies for like services under like conditions, than they are allowed to charge in eastern Canada. That principle has been applied to the carrying
of passengers, but it has not been applied to the carrying of freight. The proposal that it should apply to the carrying of freight was rejected by the government; it was declared that the Railway Commission must deal with this matter, that the responsibility was with the Railway Commission and not with the government or with parliament. Now, on behalf of the western country, I want to say that what is important to them is that they shall have a square and even deal; they ask for no advantage, but they do ask that in a question of railway transportation, which is more important to them even than the question of tariff, they shall not be discriminated against by the railway companies. And they look to parliament, which charters the railways and grants them bonuses and assistance of various kinds, and they look to the government, to see that justice is done in that particular. But the government does not want to take the responsibility. It has a Railway Commission that takes that responsibility off its shoulders. This is a form of government by commission, of which, it seems to me, it is quite possible to have a little too' much. When a great injustice exists-or I will not say injustice, but when a great and manifest inequality exists-as between the east and the west, and the government refuses to take cognizance of that condition, it is no wonder that my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett), my hon. friend from St. Antoine, Montreal (Mr. Ames), my hon friend from Brandon (Mr. Aikins), and. some other members of the House supporting the government go out through the country and make what I must characterize as very wild statements in regard to the condition of public feeling in that country. But the government surely will recognize that when their supporters are so fully impressed with the conditions as to cause them to make these statements, it is surely time for the government to take a day off from slaughtering Grit officials and pay a little atention to the necessities of the country, even though it be the western country.
While the government did not have time to deal with the grain blockade, and did not have the inclination to exercise its responsibility in dealing with the freight rates, there was one matter that they did not lose any time in dealing with. I refer to the duties on lumber. I have not the calendar at hand, but I do not think the government had been in office, more than a few days when their friends of the lumber combine in British Columbia came down and, at their demand, the lumber duties were practically readjusted so as to lay a heavier burden upon the western settler than he had borne up to that time. It was not enough that he had a bad season; it was not enough that he was

compelled to accept panic prices for his grain owing t-o the grain blockade; it was not enough that he should have to pay excessive local rates in securing a local market for his damaged grain, but our friends opposite had plenty of time to make a little adjustment of the lumber duties so as to take I should fancy not less than a quarter of a million dollars out of his pocket in this particular season, at the command of the British Columbia lumber combine.
Did I say the government did not have time? Well, in some things they had time. The _ government brought in, early in the session, a Bill to deal with the grain trade. This Bill represented the mind of the people of the west, of the producers of the west, in regard to the handling of their product. It was the result of years and years of consideration, possibly of agitation and demonstration. They came to parliament last year-came, may I say, to a friendly government-and asked that the conditions surrounding the grain trade be further improved in their interest. The Bill was prepared and was brought before parliament, but it failed to become law owing to the dissolution. It was brought forward again at this session, practically identically the same Bill. But our friends opposite had time to amend it in such shape that even my hon. friends from Lisgar (Mr. Sharpe) and Souris (Mr. Schaffner) could not, or dared not vote for its provisions. Now, Mr. Speaker, this is probably the most serious matter that has touched the west at the hands of this government since they took office. In one particular, in the matter of car distribution-and I do not intend to trouble the House with details-the Bill as it had been presented meant an average of from 2 cents to 6 cents a bushel to the western farmer selling his grain at country points. By reason of that ear distribution clause, he was able to sell his grain at the terminal, and so he could benefit by the buying competition in Winnipeg while otherwise he would have had to take the competition at the local point. And any man who knows anything of the grain trade will realize that the difference between the competition in price at country points and at the central or terminal point would mean anywhere from 2 cents to 6 cents per bushel. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) has Seen fit to amend that Act. That Act, affecting a right established by the efforts of so many years and which was of such benefit to the producer, has been framed in such a way, that, as I have said, two of the hon. gentleman's own supporters would not or could not voce for it. And there is another amendment dealing with the mixing of grain. If there is one thing more than another that the Mr. OLIVER.
farmer has insisted upon it is that the grain shall go forward to its ultimate destination under the government certificate that is given at the inspection. Again it is not necessary to deal in detail with this matter; but it is a fact that the prevention of the mixing of grain offers a premium to the good farmer and that to permit the mixing of grain destroys the good farmer's premium on the market.
My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) did not hesitate at short notice to push his amendment through which legalizes the mixing of western grades on their way to market, provides means and machinery and legalizes the degrading of the quality of western wheat as .it goes to the ultimate market.
Sir, is it any wonder that our friends behind the ministry have taken alarm? Is it any wonder that they have become 'afraid of the . consequences, first of ignoring, and then of attacking the interests of the producers of the west? I am at a loss to know on what principle this government proposes to govern this country, if it is to ignore the welfare and progress of that vast western country, if it is to ignore the importance to the whole Dominion of providing that the western farmer shall get the last cent of value of his bushel of wheat. Unless the government acts on the principle that it is necessary to recognize that right of the farmer, I am doubtful of the progress of this country in the future. It is not a question as between the east and the west, it is a question as to the whole country. If this country has progressed, if manufactures have increased in Montreal, Toronto, Hamilton and Brantford, if the price of real estate in Montreal and Toronto is high, and soaring, everybody knows that it is not because of the increase of production on the farms of Ontario and Quebec, but it is because of the increase of production in the prairie west, and that increase of production depends upon the price the farmer can get for his product. But instead of recognizing that fact, instead of bending their energies to some policy or principle that would improve the conditions of the farmer there, they come here and preach us sermons on the necessity and desirability of the farmer being on good terms with the elevator men, and not finding fault with the railroad company. They tell us that the farmer must go into mixed farming, that they are going to build the Hudson Bay railway, and that the farmer ought to be optimistic. They tell him anything and everything except what will be to the point and) will do him some good. Now let me say that it is no business of

the government whether the farmer raises ducks or raises wheat. It is his business what he raises, and they can depend upon it that he is going to raise that which is within his means and to the best advantage. It is the business of the. government to see that the best possible opportunity is given to the farmer to get the best price for what he raises. It is not a question of the railroad companies, nobody is attacking the railroad companies because they did not haul more grain than they did. The railroad companies no doubt hauled all the grain they were able to haul, along the routes that this government have allowed them to haul it. The railroad companies apparently were deprived of the advantage of taking the shorter haul, and to-day are doing the best they can to catch up with the conditions which, I am sorry to say, have been allowed to remain so long that there is no possibility now of relieving them to the full extent.
Now Sir, we are dealing with the presentation by the government of its financial propositions for the year. We are glad that they have decided to continue the tariff that has been in force for some years past. We are glad that they have declared they are going to continue the policy of [DOT]constructive development that has been the policy of the late government during past years. But if they are going to take the position that because the country is prosperous that all they have to do is to shake the plum tree vigorously, then I want to assure them that they are under a wrong impression. This condition of .prosperity that we enjoy today did not come about only as an act of Providence.
