It was necessary to give direction and inspiration to the energy and industry of our people, and because that direction was given in due course and at proper times by the late government, under its well defined policy of lower taxes and freer trade, it has been possible for this country to achieve in the current year its greatest revenue, its greatest surplus, and the greatest measure of prosperity that it has ever enjoyed. If our hon. friends are able to keep that record, if they are able to increase still further the prosperity of the country and its development, it matters not, I am free to admit, whether it is their policy or ours, whether it is high taxation or low taxation, whether i.t is restrictive trade or expanded trade. If they can secure that continued increase of prosperity with a policy of high taxation ana restricted trade, we will be glad to enjoy the prosperity and to share it with them, and we will give them the credit of their policy being better than we expected. But our belief is that this country needs a policy of lower taxes and expansion of trade,
in order to secure its continued development and prosperity.

Coming as I do from an industrial city in the province of Ontario, I think it is proper that I should say a few words on the issues raised by the budget speech presented yesterday by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. White). At the outset I desire to compliment that hon. gentleman on the exceedingly straightforward manner in which he presented the condition of the finances of this country, indicating a grasp of the financial arrangements, a grasp of expenditures and receipts, and the management of sinking funds, loan accounts, and all other subjects dealt with in the budget, which showed him to possess a master hand.
I desire, therefore, to compliment him in that way. Having said that much I must add that I have one or two regrets in regard to ithe budget speech; not for any thing that it did contain, but for one or two items of considerable importance that it did not contain. I may probably be standing in a somewhat isolated position with regard to what I have in my mind, but, being a man of business and always having been accustomed to say exactly what I mean on any given question, I propose to name the subject on which I regret that the Minister of Finance, and those who are associated with him, did1 not see fit to speak. The omission I desire to mention is the non-introduction of the iron and steel bounties. I think that the * Citizen ' this morning indicates very largely what the country thinks, that is, that the chief point that was expected was missed, because the first head line contained these words:	'No iron or steel
bounties.'
Hear, hear.

Hon. gentlemen seem to say ' all right,' but we. .are in this anomalous position, Mr. Speaker, that the iron and steel trade for the past 15 years have received more from a so-called free trade government than they are going to receive this year, and next from a so-called protectionist government. That is an anomaly that is worthy of being pointed out, and I regret that in this respect I do not agree with the budget speech that has been delivered. When a man is drowning is not the time to investigate; it is the time to save, and after that, if you wish, to find out how he got there, make inquiry. Do not wait 'while he drowns, but lend him a helping hand. If the iron and steel trade require reasonable bounties, as I believe they do, in my judgment they should be granted now', and after the Tariff Commis-

sion have made their inquiry, if it is found that they do not need this assistance, they can be taken away. How much would it have taken? According to the ' Monetary Times,' it would have taken about $2,000,000 a year. That is a very small matter,, and it may be said1 that it means very little to the industries of the country. But I would point out that it is an indication, to a certain extent, of the forces that are in control at the present time of the trade of Canada, and I quite agree that the present government were elected very largely because they were supposed to be a protectionist government.
That is my view, that is the doctrine that I preached on the hustings, and that is what I say here. I am not ashamed to own that I am a protectionist, and that I have been consistently a protectionist for thirty years past. I was brought up as a business man, I have made a special study of tariffs and business matters, and when I speak to you, Mr. Speaker, and the members of this House, I speak as a business man not desiring particularly to make any political capital at the expense of any one else, but with a true desire to look at what I believe to be the best interests of Canada in all respects, and to all classes. Remember, I am not a protectionist for the manufacturer any more than I am for the agriculturist. I know that an hon gentletnan across the way will say that you cannot) protect the agriculturist, but if he comes down to our town, or to our part of the province of Ontario, I can show him that the farmer is protected there. I can show him that the farmer of Ontario is protected to-day. He knows it and, further, he appreciates it. The farmers of Ontario at the last general election voted in very large measure for the return of this government to power, because they realised that the home market was their best market, and that it was for their welfare that it should be retained.
I also desire to call the attention of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance to the very large excess of imports over exports at the present time. I look upon that as a danger point. No less a financial authority than Sir B. E. Walker of Toronto, drew attention to it in his recent report to the shareholders of the Bank of Commerce. He says that is a danger point, and I think that in a country such as Canada, with natural resources such as she has, it requires no explanation to show that when you import, as you did last year, $472,000,000, and only export $297,000,000, there is something wrong. That is a difference of $175,000,000 between imports and exports, and that balance, for the most part, has to be settled by cash. Last year, in the trade between Mr. COCKSHUTT.
Canada and the United States, it took $165,000,000 in cash to settle the balance of trade. The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), who has just spoken, told us that it is broader markets that we are perishing for, that it is wider markets that we are suffering for, and he goes on to figure out that the western country has lost $10,000,000 by reason of reciprocity not being put into force as it would have been, according to the hon. gentleman, by the late government. I want him to make all fair deductions from that, and if he does he will find that he has a large balance on the other side, and I can show it. That reciprocity agreement did not cover grain only; it covered animals and their products, vegetables and fruits and almost every conceivable product of the farm. The hon. member for Edmonton figures out that we lost about $10,000,000 this year because we did not adopt reciprocity in so far as western grain is concerned. Let me tell him what would have happened in Ontario, Quebec and the maritime provinces. You have in these provinces one and a half million cattle, and the figures produced during the discussion of the subject proved that on cattle alone you would have had a loss of $10 a head, as compared with the value in the United States. It was figured that there would be a loss of $10 per head on milch cows, $5 to $10 per head on young cattle, and $2 to $3 per head on sheep. On cattle and sheep, Ontario, Quebec and the maritime provinces would have lost double the $10,000,000 if reciprocity had been adopted, that the hon. gentleman estimates was lost by the people of the western country on account of the refusal to adopt reciprocity. Has he no sympathy with the farmers of the east? Ontario is doing a little farming still, Ontario contains as many farmers yet as the whole of the three new provinces of the west, and Ontario for the past three years has grown more products upon its farms than have been grown in the three great western provinces. I am saying that with no disrespect to the west, but I want the hon. member for Edmonton to have a little more desire to equalize things than he appears to have, and not be ready to sacrifice the farmers of the east for the sake of the farmers of the west.
There must be give and take in this matter, and I say to the hon. member that we saved the farmers of Canada when we turned down reciprocity. If there ever was a gold brick that came down the pike, it was that reciprocity gold brick that my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) has advocated. Reciprocity was discussed in this House of Commons for six months, and I read the speeches, and high prices for the farmer was the cry that rang from one end of the Liberal benches to the other. But, when

these gentlemen got out on the hustings of Ontario, their crop was: Cheap food for the workingman. Oh, what a fall was there, from high prices for the farmer to cheap food for the working man, and so to-day wTe have in this House the hon. member from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), and the labour member from Montreal (Mr. Verville) both on the same side of the House and each advocating, an entirely different policy. But, from this side of the House, comes a policy which benefits all classes in this country; protection for both these great interests, protection for the agricultural industry and protection for manufacturing enterprises. That is the policy that has built up Canada in the past, and that is the policy that will make Canada great in the future. Reciprocity with the United States was turned down because it was a gold brick and everybody in our district knew it, and we discussed it fairly and squarely. We showed the people exactly where they would be at if they voted for reciprocity, and the farmers from one end of Ontario to the other said: We don't want any of your reciprocity; we appreciate our home markets. We were told to-night by one hon. gentleman of the opposition that it is the middleman that is causing all the trouble and that he steps in between the farmer and the consumer of the farm produce, and keeps the farmer from getting the high prices he otherwise would. Well, let me tell that hon. member what happens in my own town. I live in the city of Brantford, which has a population of about twenty-five thousand, and which, I think, is about equal to the population of the city of Edmonton. We don't make quite as much blow, and you don't hear as much about us, but we are there all the same, and I think we are producing more than does the city whence the hon. member (Mr. Oliver) comes. I may claim at all events that the city of Brantford is at least the equal of the city of Edmonton, although it is true we are content with a hundred dollars a foot for our real estate, while the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) would ask a thousand dollars a foot for real estate in his city. At all events, we have built up in the city of Brantford with great trouble and care a body of skilled labour, represented by six thousand five hundred workingmen who have been trained in their business. And with great capital and with skilled labour a great manufacturing industry has been established in the heart of an agricultural district such as Brant county is. Let me tell the hon. member how we do business in Brantford, and then he will see that the farmer gets full price for his products and that no middleman intervenes. We have a market square occupying about two acres in the centre of the city, and on
Saturday morning there are from three hundred to five hundred farmers with their wagons around that square, and these wagons are filled with the products of the farm. The workingman from the factory marches up to the farmer's wagon, laden with eggs, butter, meats of all kinds, poultry, vegetables and fruit, and he buys direct from the farmer who produces, and the money that is paid goes directly into the farmer's pocket. Is not that the right system; is not that cooperation between the country and the city? And let me tell the hon. member further, some of the prices that have obtained right in the city of Brantford under these conditions this winter: eggs have brought for the last two months from forty cents to fifty cents a dozen direct from the farmer; butter has brought from thirty cents to forty cents a pound; potatoes have brought from one dollar and fifty to two dollars a bag and so on with the other products of the farm sold direct from the farmer to the workingman, and no middleman about it. And, Mr. Speaker, what is the result:	The farmer is
prosperous and the workingman is happy and living well and enjoying himself and getting good wages in an occupation that suits him well. The workingman is saving money and the farmer is saving money, and these conditions prevailed last summer during the election campaign and, therefore, the farmers of Brant county and the workingmen in Brantford decided to let well enough alone, and they did let it alone with a vengeance; and a city that has been usually Liberal gave me almost one thousand majority, a thing I never dreamed of and never expected to see. These were the conditions that prevailed not only in Brant county but throughout the province of Ontario, and instead of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) wondering how it was all done, if he had kept up another month or two with the style of argument he has put up to-night and which was put up during the campaign, there would not have been even thirteen members from the province of Ontario. What a tumble it was from high prices for the farmer to cheap food for the workingman. The first man to make the leap from the high prices for the farmer to cheap food for the workingman was the late member the hon. Mackenzie King, who prepared the figures for the government to prove that the American market was going to be a bonanza, but as soon as he saw the figures he flopped over and he took every one with him who could be stampeded, and the ' Expositor,' the Liberal newspaper, and the ' Expositor ' man who was the candidate against me went with him in the jump. Then, instead of talking high
What about barley?

They export barley. They may not export No. 1 malting barley, but they export barley. They export potatoes, they export wheat, they export oats, they export cattle, sheep, horses, butter, cheese and all the products of the dairy. Probably, I might include flax as an export from the United States, but that may be questionable as it depends on their requirements at home, and some years they export it and some years they do not. But, take almost every product of the farm and you will find that the American is an exporter.
Including hay.

Yes, including hay. The Americans export every -class of vegetables, and in the city of Brantford, which is in the heart of an agricultural district, we are eating products of the American farms that have paid 30 per cent duty. Irish potatoes, I understand, have reached Ottawa, paying 30 per cent. Butter has reached here from the Antipodes; mutton Mr. COCKSHUTT.
has come from the Antipodes; eggs have come from Russia, China and Japan. And yet these gentlemen are teding us that we are pining and dying for broader markets, when they cannot look after the markets right here at our own doors.

Will the hon. gentleman tell the House, if the agreement had been passed and the duties on the articles he has mentioned had been taken off, would that have increased or decreased the cost of living in Canada?
Would it have increased the price to the farmer?

I think that in some lines it would have decreased the cost of living at certain times of the year; but I want to say further that we in the city, realizing the climatic conditions in this country, knowing the difficulties that our farmers have in producing their stuff in the cold weather, are ready to pay a fair price so as to give them a profit in order to remain on the land. My hon. friend will see eggs coming from the United States, where the chickens run free all winter, and compete with eggs laid by hens in a pen artificially heated and where every bit of food has to be provided. Is that a fair proposition? My hon. friend would admit the vegetables grown by negro labour in the southern states at this time of the year when our vegetables have to be grown under glass. He would have our vegetable producer, who has to heat his hothouse with' coal at $7 or $8 a ton, compete with southern labour, which can grow vegetables in the open air. I would be prepared to meet my hon. friend before any audience of farmers, and I would make him take back many of the arguments he has put forward to-night.
If my hon. friend will permit me, I want to say most distinctly that my policy is free food, so long as we can get free markets for the food we export.

My policy in opposition to that is to give every man a chance to live, and live well. I know that in Canada industry cannot thrive without protection, that the Ontario farmer cannot thrive as he is thriving without protection; and if my hon. friend does not know that, he ought to know it before he undertakes to speak for the farmers of Canada. What does the proposition of my hon. friend mean? It means that not only the products of the United States, of which there are hundreds of millions in excess every year, but the products of Russia, of China, of Japan, of Norway, of Sweden, of Denmark, of Australia, of New Zealand, Argentina, and other parts of the world, would be dumped in Canada to compete against those of our farmers, and without a single conces-

ision from those countries. If there ever was a jug-handled proposition if there ever was a policy propounded by men whom Providence led on . to destruction, it was the policy propounded by the Laurier government. We are sorry for the two old gentlemen who went to Washington and came back with that gold brick, and we are sorry for the men who sent them; but if they were foolish enough to take so foolish a course, we say now gentlemen take your medicine, and the longer you hammer away at reciprocity, the longer you will stay on that side of the House. We are glad to have you talk reciprocity, and we will meet you all along the line on every argument you can make. There is not a single argument in the whole list with regard to which we cannot justify a protective policy for Canada. The hon. gentleman's party were in the government for 15 years, during which they came very near to practising die National Policy, and wherever they deflected from that policy they made a mistake. Now, I am not speaking at random. Let me give two instances. When the hon. gentleman's party came into power there were flourishing in Canada twelve barbed-wire factories. They had not been in office two years before they removed the duty on barbed-wire, and since then for years there has not been one pound of barbed-wire manufactured in Canada. Take hinder twine, of which there are two industries struggling in Brantford at present. The hon. gentleman's party took the duty off binder twine. I am not discussing whether or not that was an act of wisdom; but I am showing how reciprocity of that kind works. The price of binder twine went up, and all the twelve factories but three are now gone. Of these three factories, one that had $3,000,000 capital has cut it down to $1,000,000, and the other two are struggling for life, and may not last until the Tariff Commission comes to their relief.
Hear, hear.

Hon. gentlemen laugh. They have laughed before it was time to laugh. They are a good deal in the position of the Irishman who was handed a shillelah. He asked, 'What shall I do with this? This man who gave it to him said, ' Wherever you see a head, hit it.' That is what hon. gentlemen opposite would like to do: wherever they see a struggling industry, they want to hit it on the head-why should it flourish? If it loses money, they do not say anything, but let it go; but if it is making money, it is a mark for the shillelah of our hon. friends. The hon. member for Edmonton since last September has repeated at least a thousand times some of the expressions he has given utterance to to-163
night. I am within the mark when I say that he has repeated the words * mergers, combines and trusts,' at least a thousand times. Has he destroyed one of them? No, but he is doing his best to destroy his party. He is doing his utmost to raise the west against the east. He is telling us in the east that we have no problems that should have attention. The hon. gentleman forgets that Canada is more than a mere province or a city like Edmonton. We wish Edmonton every success; we are proud of it. I visit it with great satisfaction. I do not know whether or not my hon. friend has spent in the west more than I have if he has, I would be surprised to hear it. My interests are bound up in the west as much as those of my hon. friend, and I would not lift my finger to injure any western interest. I trust that I am too broad a man to endeavour to have a policy which' would be good only for my town or my riding, and would let the rest of the country go to the dogs. I hope, as the years go by, that my hon. friend will take a broader view of this country, that he will consider what it is from the Atlantic to the Pacific, that he will not forget our brethren down by the sea, who are men of the right stock, and who, if they have done nothing else, have given to the west some of the very best blood that it has to-day. A country that can raise such men is worth keeping. We have not been inimical to the interests of the maritime provinces. We have scarcely had an opportunity to get a man to settle in the eastern provinces.
To what industry was the hon. gentleman referring in the maritime provinces?

Agriculture particularly. I think my hon. friend is rejoicing in the disappearance of the iron and steel bounties. He certainly approved of that course, and this emphasizes my fear with regard to it, because I always shun anything that my hon. friend endorses. I am sure I am on the right track if I am opposed to the hon. gentleman. That is the reason I feel so sure. The iron and steel bounties are of great importance to Nova Scotia, I think even some of his1 own political friends will endtorse that. For 15 years the hon. gentlemen himself endorsed these bounties when his government gave them. Now he congratulates the country because these bounties have disappeared as soon as the late government are out of power, and he is willing to sacrifice Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Quebec, because he thinks this little $2,000,000 that is going to be saved to the pockets of Canada is far more important than that these industries should go on and flourish. He is not so slow to commit us to large ex-



penditures when he thinks they will be of any advantage to himself or his part of the country. I understand1 he has both hands up for the Hudson Bay railway. We certainly have an overflowing treasury, and I think that this is a time for expansion, but there are many of us in the east who have our misgivings as to the propriety of rushing ahead with that road.
The west is going to pay for that road, and is not asking the east for any money for it.
I had not heard of that. How is the west proposing to pay for it?
By the sate of land.

The non. gentleman says the people of the west are proposing to take all the risk with regard to it. Of course if they are building the road with their own money all well and good'. I thought it was to be for the general advantage of Canada, and that the expense would come out of the general funds of the country. The hon. gentleman admits that he asks the government to assume the control and operation of terminal elevators, which would involve an enormous expenditure. I hold up both hands for all matters of that kind that will help the west, but if $2,000,000 is going to save industries in the east, and my hon. friend1 wants $20,000,000 or $30,000,000 or $50,000,000 for the west, does be not think it would be rather kind of him to allow us to spend a million or two in the east if we spend $10,000,000 or $20,000,000 at his behest for the benefit of the west? I do not know if the hon. gentleman would go that far with me or not, but I trust he will, and I trust he will admit that these things which affect the east should be encouraged as well as those things which affect the west. But I shall not pursue the hon. gentleman in that course any further.
I have talked on reciprocity. I have shown you the reasons we turned it down, and1 turned it down hard, and we showed the people of the province of Ontario a more excellent way. My hon. friend may say what do you mean, you denied us access to the markets of the United States which were already overflowing with all the products of all kinds that Canada could possibly send to them. We have had something else in mind besides that when we turned down reciprocity. We said to our friends in Ontario that we believed reciprocity was dangerous from a material, a National and an Imperial standpoint. In a material sense we proved our case up to the hilt to the satisfaction of the farmer and the working man. Then we took the Mr. COCKSHUTT.
national view, and we said that reciprocity would strike a staggering blow at confederation, because when the Dominion was formed one of the conditions of the union was the construction of railways to run east and west in order to bring the provinces into' touch, and to secure the flowing of trade east and west between them. My hon. friend wants to stop all that, to take the wheels off those railways running east and west, and to rim his into the United States which is already flooded with these products. What would that have meant? The diversion of the carrying trade of the great west into New York, Boston and {Portland. These ports would handle the traffic that should have gone from our own Atlantic and Pacific ports,
Would my hon. friend tell me how he can possibly make out that the railways running north and south would have taken our products to a place which is already flooded with them?

I think the proposition is dead easy and I am sorry my hon. friend has not been able to see it. He comes from a country where they do not see things quite as quickly as we do in Canada. The products of the northwest would flow in at say North Portal into Illinois, Dakota and Minnesota, and the same products would flow out over the American roads through Boston, Portland, and New York. The hon. gentleman may ask how I know that. The American statistics show that they are exporting from all these ports every item that we could send into the United States. They might eat a little Canadian grain but then they would have all the more American grain to export. Every bushel of wheat thar entered the United States from the Northwest territories, would displace a bushel of American wheat to go to the markets of Europe to compete with us in the great British market which we at present enjoy. These hon. gentlemen have built up a beautiful theory. They say: Broader markets, what we want is beautiful broad markets.
My hon. friend says that because the United States exports wheat there is therefore no market in the United States for Canadian wheat. Does the hon. gentleman say the same thing in regard to ploughs?

In regard to a certain kind of plough yes, if you make the best plough in the world you will get a few into the United States. Let me tell my hon. friend that this is a free country and if he thinks there is money in making ploughs I invite him to go into the business. I think he will soon conclude that

No. 1 Hard wheat is a better proposition than plough making. He will be quiie welcome. We have no monopoly, it is an open free market for everyone who wants to come in, and if my hon. friend says he wants to enter the competition, all right. I say that if the United States has a surplus of produce, then for every bushel of Canadian wheat that is sent in there and consumed by the American people there is a bushel more of American grain to export. A blind man can see that proposition. A market which is full cannot be more than full, and the United States is replete with every class of foodstuffs produced at first hand, in many cases cheaper than we can produce them. Why? Climatic conditions are at the root of the situation and I say that the farmer who with great difficulty raises early lambs in this country in artificially heated barns is entitled to receive for those lambs a higher price than the man who raises lambs in Alabama or Texas where they can run out in grass all the year round and require no hand feeding.
And you ask the farmers of Canada to compete with such a country as that. We are willing that the farmer shall get high prices. How high? As high as will pay him to stay upon the farm. And the workingmen of Canada are willing to pay it. Why? Because the manufacturers have been prosperous and have paid their workingmen accordingly. When the National Policy was introduced in 1878 men were getting from 85 cents to $1 a day. They are now getting $1.75 to $2 for even the cheapest labour in Canada, while artisans are making from $3 to $4 and' even $5 a day throughout this country. And the workingman knows, if my hon. friend does not, that protection has a lot to do with it.
. Now the hon. gentleman disturbed me in my argument and I wish to go on as rapidly as possible, because I have a big subject to deal with and do not wish to weary the House. I say that we turned down reciprocity, and in doing so we showed to Canada a yet more excellent way. And what is that way? Trade with the mother country on preferential rates and advantageous terms. That is what we said, and that is the secret that more than anything else destroyed the late government. We got the people of Canada to see it; even though my hon. friend does not see it yet. The former Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) came down to Simcoe, the county town adjoining my native county of Norfolk-and that was the only win he made in Ontario and he did it this way. He said to the people: They say that this reciprocity arrangement will injure the preference; don't you believe it; we are the men who gave the 163i
preference and we stand by it, and the preference cannot be hurt by this arrangement. Never was a more fallacious statement set before any audience than that if made to men who know what trade preference means. The policy of a British preference was not inaugurated by hon. gentlemen opposite as they have always claimed. I make that statement advisedly. The first preference proposed ever laid before the empire in a public way was made by the great statesman who has been lying almost at death's door this winter, Sir Charles Tupper, whose name has been a household word for so long in Canada. He was the first man to introduce ithe doctrine of preference and not the jughandled variety of preference adopted by hon. gentlemen opposite. The preference that Sir Charles Tupper and those who followed him advocated was a give and take policy, and to this I invite especially the attention of my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark). I say that the preference we advocate and we ask the people of Canada to turn to was not the jug-handled preference now in force, but a preference ir. which we would receive something for something given. What would this reciprocity have done had it been endorsed? It would have destroyed the possibility forever of having a preference arranged with the mother country such as is proposed. Everybody can see that; it is plain on the face of it-there could have been no mutual preferential arrangement with the old country if reciprocity had come into force. Why, reciprocity was aimed at that. J. J. Hill made no secret of it. He said:	Gentlemen, there is a
move on foot in Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, along with Great Britain, to make a great trade compact whereby the mother country will receive from the colonies a preferential rate on the foodstuffs they have to send. Reciprocity, on the other hand, would have permitted the American wheat to come into the Canadian market free of duty. Now, can my hon. friends opposite tell me how Canadian wheat could get preferential treatment in the British market where the American wheat was coming in free, without giving the same treatment to the United States? And to give it to the United States would be to destroy the inter-imperial preference. They are looking to the idea that Canadian wheat will receive preference in the British market. And I take issue with the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) in	what he said on the
subject in this debate. I tell that hon. gentleman, and I tell any other hon. member on that side that the tariff reform movement, the empire preferential movement, i3 yet going to be the winning card-and under a Canadian Pre-

mier, too, Mr. Bonar Law. I believe that will be the fixed policy. I believe it to be a ' comer ' and that it will afford to Britain and the empire a bond such as we have never seen in the history of the world. That is the more excellent way pointed out to our northwest friends-not to trade less with the United St ites, but to trade more with the mother country. The mother country requires over 180,000,000 bushels of imported wheat-more than the northwest is yet able to supply. And the United States is getting more of that market to-day than we are. These gentlemen in England tell us that they are prepared, as soon as they get into power, to arrange a preferential agreement with Canada, New Zealand and South Africa by which the products of the farms of this country will be received into Great Britain at preferential rates. That is not an impossibility; that was practised sixty years ago. And it was a success then and will be a success in the future. I see that my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) does not appreciate that statement. But I think he will realise, if he consults the history of that period that it is quite true that there was prosperity of the empire before the Cobden days-which were intended to smash the empire; Richard Cobden made no bones about it, he said, free trade will ultimately cause a disunion of the empire; that is the doctrine he preached when he introduced free trade and broke the preference to do it. Canada had a preference in Great Britain in timber, raw products and foodstuffs. That is a well known fact of history; and before Richard Cobden appeared on the scene the empire was thriving better than it has ever done since. Let us look at the picture there to-day, and I say this with the deepest sympathy. Every man in this House regrets from the bottom of his heart the affliction that has fallen upon the mother country during the last two weeks, where upwards of a million miners are on strike and most of the industrial concerns of the country are closing down. I say our hearts go out in sympathy to them in their affliction; we realize that Great Britain is in the throes of great trouble. But we are ready to stand by the same policy that we have proposed for twenty-five years past if I understand aright. I understand that this government is recognized as a government that has an Imperial policy, and I say that now is the time to bring that policy to the front. And that is the reason, more particularly, why I speak to-night. I say, I pin my faith to the union of the British Empire- union in trade and union in defence. And we cannot bring that about too soon. That is the reason why the United States was so anxious to detach Canada from the Imperial orbit. For, detach Canada and Mr. COOKSHUTT.
you break the chain. That was the idea, and J. J. Hill knew it and preached it. He said:	Now is the accepted time, now
is the time to break the chain-now, or never. But we got the people of Canada to see it; and the people of Canada did see it and said: Whether the bargain with the United States is good or not, our duty is to the mother country first and to the dominions overseas. They said that and they voted that, and the lesult is that hon. gentlemen then in power aTe on the opposition side of the House to-night. The policy announced by the Right Hon. Joseph Chamberlain about ten years ago is the endorsed policy of the business men of the empire. My hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) says there is nothing to it. I am sorry he is not in the House to hear me read a resolution I have here, but he can see it in ' Hansard.' This is the businessmen's views as expressed on three different occasions in the greatest trade gatherings that have ever taken place in the British Empire. This gathering took place in Montreal, the convention of the Chambers of the Empire in 1903. And I now read the resolution that was passed, at that time:
It i9 resolved that in the opinion of this Congress the bonds of the British Empire would be materially strengthened, and the union of the various parts of His Majesty's Dominions greatly consolidated by the adoption of a commercial policy based upon the principles of mutual benefits, whereby each component part of the empire, would receive a substantial advantage in trade as a result of its national relationship, due consideration being given to the fiscal needs of the component parts of the Empire.
That this Congress urges upon His Majesty's government the appointment by them of a special commission composed of representatives of Great Britain and her colonies and India to consider the possibilities of thus increasing and strengthening the trade relations between the different parts of the Empire and the trading facilities within the Empire, and with foreign countries.
Now, that resolution was passed by a very large vote of picked business men of the whole empire that went to London in 1906, where, convened with the majority of the British Chamber of Commerce, (they passed a similar resolution in the heart of the empire. Three years ago they went to Australia, my hon. friend from Montreal (Mr. Ames) and myself being Canadian delegates, and in Sydney they again passed a Jsimilar resolution. So three times over a congress of the Chambers of Commerce of the empire has decided that an empire combination in behalf of trade is what is wanted. That is my policy. I have advocated that policy for 25 years, and I am advocating it here to-night. I say that is what will give a better price

to our farmers and our workingmen. The United States wishes also to become a parftaker in the benefits of that polidy which will give the Northwest a great deal more money for its wheat. The British market is the market that pays the beat, because Great Britain requires an immense amount of that kind of stuff from this side of the world. She is naturally inclined to trade with Canada to the best advantage, and it is natural that she would be more generous toward her own children than to strangers. That is a policy of empire preference. 1 believe that ere long we will see Great Britain and her colonies united in one confederation for the benefit of the whole empire, co-operating entirely in trade and defence. When that happy day comes I believe we will have accomplished the greatest work the world has ever known in empire building. We will never be united as we should be until that combination is complete. We wish to see the British workingman for his own sake receive the same benefit that the workingman in Canada receives. We are sorry to-day for these coal miners. I think if there is one class in the community with whom we should sympathize more than another, it is the coal miner who has to leave the world of light and go down in the bowels of the earth, and at the risk of his life delve and dig there in order that we might be kept warm through the winter. I say our hearts go out in sympathy to him, we think it is a pity he is not better paid in the mother country; we realize that they want something in the shape of protection, so that the employing classes may be able to pay better wages. In the words of a miner's song:
Mammon i9 the master and man is the slave.
Toiling for wealth on the brink of the grave
Leaving the world of sunlight and sound
For the darkmes of night and a silence profound.
For the man that delves in the coal mines our hearts go out in sympathy. And if we could1 send a sympathetic message to Great Britain that we are prepared to stand by her, to make a bargain with her to lock our trade with her own, and our business interests with hers, we would be doing something great and grand that would redound to the credit of Canada, and I trust the time is not far distant when we shall take that step. I sympathised1 thoroughly last night with the member for South York (Mr. Maclean), who spoke on the naval question, I sympathise with him in that respect as well as on the trade question. I know that this is not the occasion to dwell on that subject, but I may say that if we are true Britishers we shall see to it that in
trade and defence we will give the best we have, the best help, and the best consideration to the mother country, and to the sister colonies of Australia, New Zealand, and South Africa in every respect that we can.
Now, Sir, I have spoken longer than I intended. So far as I am concerned, I stand for a policy that will build up every interest and' every part of Canada. I do not want to see the east built up at the expense of the west, nor the west built up at the expense of the east. 1 want to see the west and the east stand by one another like brothers, that is the way 1 feel, and if at any time anybody has ever drawn any other construction from my remarks he has done me an injustice. I stand as firmly in my desire for the welfare of the west as for the welfare of the east. I have a son of my own in the west, I have interests in the west, and I am just as heartily desirous of the success of the west as I am of the east. But I say we must have a give and take policy in this matter, we must stand together to develop the country. One part cannot grow without assisting the other. We must be united in a policy of development, in a policy that will be not a hindrance to any parr, but a policy of co-operation, giving earnest heed for the welfare of every part of this vast country.

First of all I wish to congratulate the Minister of Finance on the very systematic and capable way in which he presented his budget speech. I would like to say first of all that I quite agree with him that railway subsidies should not be charged to capital account, but to consolidated fund account; I think the former Minister of Finance also expressed the same view. I remember that I had the privilege of saying so once before. I certainly congratulate the country that in 1910-11 we had a surplus of $30,000,000 in round figures, and an increase in the debt, after paying a large amount towards the Transcontinental, of only $3,773,000. I congratulate the country at-large, and more especially I think the late government, on the surplus that is shown for the financial year of 1911-12, being sufficient not only to pay all the expenses under consolidated fund account, but also the large amount that had to be paid towards the Transcontinental railway, and in implementing the bonds of that railway in the west, leaving an amount to apply on public debt of $1,150,000. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance said that he thought, and I agree with him, that to the energy and perseverance of the Canadian people is due the splendid showing he was able to make. I quite agree with
Hear, hear.

Pardon me, the hon. member for Dundas (Mr. Broder) told the member for Edmonton to-night that our late Minister of Agriculture had not done his duty towards agriculture in the older provinces, in that he neglected to see that, the

farmers raise4 large families and kept them on the land. He told us also that houses should be built for the hired men on the farms, and he promised that the present Minister of Agriculture was going to see to it that the farmers of Ontario especially would raise large families, keep them on the land, and build houses for their working men.
The hon. member (Mr. Nesbitt), has misstated1 my remarks.
I regret if that is so, but that is the way I understood my hon. friend (Mr. Broder).
You are quite wrong.
Anyway, the suggestion is an excellent one.
I simply referred to the fact that it would be wise to build houses for the hired men and let them raise their families, so as to solve the domestic help question.
I do not know that it would be wdse for the government to undertake to build houses for the -farm labourers of Ontario.
You are misquoting me again; I said the farmers themselves should do that.

Well, I think that is a very good idea. For the last ten years 1 have been urging on our farmers at home that the best way to solve the hired man problem was to build houses for them, hire them by the whole year, and keep good men when they got them.
In my experience the farm hand that we get from the old country is not at all equal to our own native product. The native-born is the man for me every time, while I find no fault with the immigrants from the old land some of whom make excellent hands. The farmers themselves can remedy the trouble very materially by building houses on their farms and hiring their hands for the year instead of for eight months, and letting them for the rest of the time go idle or go to the towns to swell the ranks of the unemployed there. Agriculture, we are told, is flourishing. I am glad to say that it flourished throughout Ontario last year, though as a matter of fact the crop was not much more than half the usual crop.
I note from the minister's speech that there are to be no changes in the tariff. As my hon. friend from Edmonton points out, while our hon. friends have been finding fault with the late government for the last fifteen years, they have not seen fit this year to change the tariff in any way. They are going to wait for the report of that wonderful Tariff Commission that is Mr. NESBITT.
going to do so much for the people of this country. I was surprised, however, that there were not some changes made. For instance, take the cement tariff. Cement is used by nearly every farmer and workingman in this country. An enormous quantity of cement is used by the farmers of Ontario. I understand that there is a Cement Combine. I am not complaining of that. I am complaining, however, that the duty on cement should be retained to the detriment of the farmer and the workingman. The workingman, if he has a home of his own, wants cement to build sidewalks to it. To the farmer cement is almost as much a necessity as food and clothing. I was surprised, therefore, that there was no intimation of an intention on the part of this government to reduce the duty on cement. Some people say that cement is no dearer in Canada than it is (in the United States. As a matter of fact, it is selling at $1.20 in Buffalo and at $1.75 in Woodstock, Hamilton and Brantford. The cement business in this country is thoroughly established, it does not need protection as an infant industry, and therefore, there is no reason why the farmers of Canada should not have been given a reduction of the duty on cement. Then, take the item of potatoes. With the price at which potatoes have been for the last four months there is no reason why hon. gentlemen opposite should not have passed an order in council remitting the duty on potatoes for a period, as they did on coal going into the west last year. I think it has been a crime to charge the poor man, or even the rich or reasonably well-off man, the duty on potatoes during the last four months. There has been no object in doing so, because we have not had potatoes for sale; we have been importing them from Ireland, from the United States and from other countries.
Now, my hon. friend from Brantford was very enthusiastic over the bounties on steel and iron. He said the late government had continued those bounties for the last 15 years. As a matter of fact, I think they were originated by the friends of the present government before the late government came into power; but we continued them and perhaps increased them. As far as I am personally concerned, I do not think the late government should have given those bounties; but in their wisdom they gave them to the iron and steel industry while it was in its infancy, and as soon as they thought that industry had grown up and was able to support itsed, they did away with the bounties. It was i ot the present government that did so. Everybody thought they were going to put on the bounties again, but apparently they dare not do so, and personally I am very pleased that this is the ease. We heard a great deal from the hon. member for

Brantford about the balance of trade, about our importing more than we export. I am not worrying about that; it shows the prosperous condition of the country. It is like a man starting in business. Before he can start he must necessarily put in a plant and equipment. The balance of trade is all against him at the start. We are oqly organizing (this country. We have grown enormously in the last 15 years. The consequence is that we have been bringing from the United States and also from England, hundreds of millions of dollars1 worth of machinery to equip our factories; and we are bringing enormous quantities of supplies from the old country. This only shows that the country is prospering, and is preparing for still greater growth in the future, as we have to provide our equipment before we can be what we shall eventually become. The balance of trade is nearly all represented by the vast quantities of machinery that we are bringing in that we cannot make ourselves, to equip our factories. My hon. friend from Brantford told us in a very enthusiastic manner that his people went to the market to buy their vegetables, fruits, meats, &c. We all know that that is done ah over Ontario; every town has its market. He asks, would you allow the cheap eggs and vegetables from the Southern States to come in and compete with our eggs and vegetables? I say yes, by all means. Would you deprive the ordinary man living in the city or the town from buying vegetables simply because he cannot pay the price for those grown under glass?
That is so far as vegetables are concerned, and as for eggs, what benefit do oar farmers get from eggs being 40 cents a dozen. When eggs are at that price there is not one in a hundred who has any eggs for sale; but when eggs come down to 20 cents and 25 cents a dozen, as they are now and have been for the last two weeks, the farmers get some benefit because they have some for sale. If vegetables go up to a high price because they are grown under glass and the ordinary residents of our towns cannot afford to buy them, does that benefit the farmers? Is that not. a, great disadvantage to the workingman? Because a darkey grows them down in Georgia, should we deprive the workingman of the benefit of being able to get potatoes and fresh vegetables in our towns and cities? What harm would that do to the potatoes or the vegetables? Yet you deprive the workingman of them. My hon. friend says that we told1 the people that under reciprocity the farmer was going to be benefited' and the workingman would get his goods cheaper. We heard that illustrated to* nteht. Mv hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Verville) showed you by figures that
were undeniable that while the raw production was dearer, the food for the family was cheaper in the United States, the farmer there got more for it. Take the figures for any part of the United States, and! you will find that the farmer does getj *more for his raw material 'and that the workingman gets his meat 'and his vegetables cheaper because the price to somebody is less. I have no fault to find with the middleman. We have got to have middlemen, but there is reason in all things, and there is no reason why eggs should be purchased for 30 cents from the farmer and1 sold at 50 cents to the consumer. At the same time, while there may have been a few eggs sold at Brantford for 40 and 50 cents a dozen, Brantford is too near Woodstock to have such a difference, as the farmers from near Woodstock would go to Brantford to get such prices, and there were no eggs sold in Woodstock this winter at over 35 cents a dozen. Even then, who got the benefit, how many were sold? One woman could carry them all on her arm, because how many people are there in Woodstock who could afford to pay 35 cents or 40 cents a dozen for eggs? My hon. friend may say that there were more people in' his ' town than in some other town able to afford such prices, but I doubt it.
As my hon. friend from Edmonton says, we would have benefited the great west in allowing them to ship their grain. What nonsense to say that because the United States is an exporting country it could not absorb this western grain. He has told you that we built railways connecting the provinces; and that if we allowed that grain to go to the south it would have stopped shipments over these railways. As a matter of fact, when we have the three Transcontinental railways in operation we will be just as badly off or nearly iso, iso far las the west is concerned, as we are to-day with reference to shipping facilities. What assistance has the Intercolonial railway been to the people in the west? Is it any benefit to the people in the west to see their grain rotting in. the fields or in the railway yards because we want to secure the shipment of that grain over the Intercolonial railway to the east? What harm would it have done us to have a tree market? The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), is absolutely right when he tells you that the farmers of the west during the last 15 years have been of the greatest possible benefit to the manufacturers of the east, and I heard last week of one court in one city in the west that during one week recently had issued 600 writs on farmers because they could not pay for implements, etc., shipped out there. That is a serious

state of affairs and that could have been helped1 last year as the hon. member for Edmonton claims it should have been helped. Would it not have been a grand thing for the people of the eastern country to have assisted them in 'this? It is quite true that the farmers of Ontario were not grumbling about the prices. It is not exactly correct to say that it was loyalty to Great Britain that defeated reciprocity among the farmers of Ontario. What tended to defeat reciprocity more than anything else in the world' was the fear that as we were getting good prices a change might not be beneficial, the eternal call of the British-born in our towns and cities and the appeal against the American who was too smart for us. I told the electors on the platform and I repeat tonight, that any Canadian who has so little pride as to think that the American is more clever than the Canadian in a business transaction I do not want to have as a fellow-Canadian. I have never yet seen any reason why we as a people, individually or collectively, should be afraid to put our brains up against our friends on the other side of the line. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Cockshutt) says that so far as the farmers in his section of the country are concerned, they were united against reciprocity. So far as the farmers in my section are concerned, and I think they are as good as there are in the world, they were very strongly in favour of reciprocity and they did not care a snap of the fingers about protection. They do not ask for protection; they can farm, and sell goods against the world and they are not afriad to produce goods and sell them against the world. I, as a farmer standing here to-night, just as much interested in farming as- any man in this country, according to my means, tell you that' I do not want your protection. I can farm and raise produce, whether it is sheep, pigs, cattle or grain, and, sell it against the world. Do not deceive yourselves into believing that the farmers of Ontario voted against reciprocity because they wanted protection. They voted against reciprocity becaues they were deceived by factional cries.
Not so.

I tell you it is so. I know what I am talking about when
I talk of the farmers of Ontario. For there is nobody here who mixes with them more than I do, and nobody here who consults with them more than I do. And that is the way to find out. My hon. friend *j'om Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) told us that when we came into power we ruined I do not know how many factories that were in the business of making barbed Mr. NESBITT.
wire. These factories got their wire from the United States-that country that we are told is so corrupt and bad-and they twisted the barbs into it in this country. No wire was made in this country; the barbed-wire was finished here, that is all. But who got the benefit of the change? The farmers got the benefit. Hon. gentlemen opposite know that. And I dare them to-night to put a duty on barbed wire. Let them do that, and they will see how long the farmers of Ontario favour such a policy. I do not wish to see any factory ruined. Everybody knows that I am in favour of reasonable protection. But there is reason in everything; and there are times when protected industries, even in their own interest, should consider the interest of the public at large. As I have said, I dare these hon. gentlemen to put a duty on barbed-wire, whether their Tariff Commission reports in favour of it or not. And the same with binder twine. We are told that the price went up after the duty was taken off. Everybody knows that the reason for that was not the taking off of the duty, but the higher price of the raw material. The binder twine factory in Brantford to which the hon. member (Mr. Cockshutt) referred, was started by the suscriptions of the farmers. It paid the farmers 80 per cent dividend the first year; the second year 40 per cent, nothing the next year, and nothing ever since. And why? Because they made money out of the rise of price of raw material and 'sold the raw material rather than make it into binder twine.
I believe the hon. gentleman (Mr. Nesbitt) has the Bain wagon factory in his constituency. Is he in favour of protection to that industry?
Certainly.
Then, why not to others?

I have just said I am in favour of that. I am in favour of reasonable protection on the Bain wagon product the same as on others. And if they cannot exist with a reasonable protection, I don't want them 'to exist at all. And I do not believe the Bain wagon people do either.
Is the hon. gentleman in favour of the present protection on wagons?
I voted for it. And the Bains voted for me and did everything in their power to elect me. And there was a reduction of the duty on wagons by the reciprocity agreement.
Is the hon. gentleman still in favour of reciprocity?

Certainly I am. There is no man in this House more willing than I am to let every class of people in this country have a living; nobody more willing that there should be reasonable protection to manufacturers so long as they require it, while industries are in their infancy. But let me tell hon. gentlemen opposite that the day is coming when this, proposition will carry in this country.
Oh, oh.

You may laugh; but it is coming. There has got to be a reduction of duties as was proposed under reciprocity. There are industries in this country that need protection, but there are other industries, and hon. gentlemen opposite know it, and none better than the Minister of Einance (Mr. White), that do not need the protection they now have. And the people pay for that protection. As I said a few minutes ago, why keep the duty on potatoes when the farmers of this country have none to sell? Why have a duty on any foodstuff? We the farmers of Ontario don't want it. We can compete; and you do not make the farmers more able to compete by a duty of 3 cents on eggs. How much barley do we in Ontario ship out except for malting purposes? We grow it only to ship out for malting purposes, because barley is not as good feed for our cattle and hogs as our other cereals that we can grow. And how much wheat do we want to sell? It has got to be in the neighbourhood of a dollar a bushel or the farmers of Ontario don't sell it; they feed it. Farming factories-that is what they are coming to be in this country. And I believe we shall see the day, when, as my hon. friend from Dundas (Mr. Broder) said, more intensive farming will be carried on in Ontario. But vve do not want your protection; that is the excuse you have for the whole system of protection; though it is not the one I make. I am perfectly frank in declaring my belief, that the infant industries of this country require a certain protection. But it should be reasonable; it should be only sufficient to allow them the difference between the cost of manufacturing in other countries and the cost of manufacturing here. And the rest should go to the consumer.
Now, I am sorry to have taken up so much time; but at least I can say that I do not often claim the attention of the House. During the last electoral campaign T [DOT]happened to make a comparison which seemed very clear to ine. The United States government, by imposing $4 duty on hay, keeps us away from the Boston and the New York markets and from the New England markets so as to *favour the farmers of the 'Western States. Mr. PAQUET (iL'Islet), Mr. 'Speaker, the hon. Finance Minister laid down very clearly yesterday the true principles of good financial administration.
The budget of 1913 comes to us as one of reform and progress, marking a new stage .on the road to financial restoration.
Laisne once gave to Mr. Villele some advice under a rough form:
A financial minister, he said should be a watch dog, lying on the national strong box.
The finance minister is following this advice and he will show us results worthy of the admirable vitality of the Canadian people.
On the evening of the 21st September some of our opponents felt anxious on account of Mr. Fielding's absence, but we know now that not only has the present finance minister (Mr. White), succeeded iMr. Fielding; he has replaced him.
Montesquieu once said: 'Certain things are accepted by the people only when unseen; as soon as they appear the people re ject them.'
During the last two sessions, on the questions of the navy and of reciprocity, the Liberal majority demonstrated the truth of the French philosopher's words. That majority, forgetful of the rights of the people, acted as if they had a general mandate and relied upon the acceptance by the public of the accomplished fact. Under Liberal rule, national representation had given way _ to uncontrolled dictatorship. The sovereignty of the people had become Mr. LANCTOT.
a farce. Our opponents thought that they had obscured the national conscience. But on the 21st September, militarism, imperialism and reciprocity went down before the rights of the people and the national policy. It was the awakening of the spirit of the nation to the necessity of protecting our national resources, our industries and our agriculture.
The lightening of the naval tax is deeply significant; the government was thus enabled to adopt manly, resolutions, and to turn earnestly towards the improvement of' agriculture and of our national highways.

The people require commercial and financial reforms adequate to the wants and aspirations of the different classes of society. Among the nations we perceive a progressive wealth of brilliant commercial institutions. In all those countries to which extend our industrial and commercial activities we require commercial agents properly trained and informed as to our resources and our economic situation. We have such agents in several countries, but progressive Canada should insist upon more complete commercial representation in this respect. Our universities and our great commercial schools, so interested in our material and intellectual development, might furnish proper agents for this commercial and consular service. They are in a position to accomplish this national work. The Department of Trade and Commerce, now administered by a distinguished man, should be in a position to collect all useful information for the development of our trade and manufactures.
This missi dominici would transmit to the central administration a mine of accurate information. In trade with the east, with France and South America, we have not obtained our full share. I cannot sufficiently impress upon our new government the importance of opening new markets to Canadian products, while preserving to the full our administrative autonomy.
Speaking of the .commercial progress of Canada, I can never sufficiently insist upon the importance of the report of the United States immigration commission. Their labour and their talents add to the wealth of our neighbours instead of enriching Canada.

In the interest of Canada we should keep our people here- and encourage the return of the French Canadian population so important on account of their traditions and its attachment to the faith of their ancestors.
Our new government will meet our wishes by the development of our industries fostered by a tariff policy framed to meet our needs, while favouring at the same time our agricultural progress. Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to take part in the debate, especially at this late hour, but I think I would be failing in my duty a>s one of 'the representatives of Montreal-the commercial metropolis of 'Canada-if I did not say a few words on the subject.
This evening when I was in the cars coming from Montreal, I learned by the papers that the hon. Minister of Finance had stated to the House that he has a surplus of 39 millions. He has had better luck than his predecessor, who, when taking office in 1896, found only -an -empty coffer and -even a deficit of $330,000.
In my division, I carried the last campaign almost exclusively on the question of reciprocity with occasionally some remarks on the naval policy.
In what condition was this country in 1896 and in what condition is it to-day? The country, and Montreal in particular, was in a lamentable state. The manufactories were closed, and the men were leaving for the United States. What was the jcause of all those disasters? For my part, I say that the real cause was the policy of protection inaugurated 'by the Conservative party in 1878 and that policy was that the farmers of this country should not produce any more than was required for home consumption. A time .came when the farmer having no market to which he could export his products, found himself with an over production that he was obliged to sell at any price. I remember the time when the!, 'farmer in ,'the province of Quebec was obliged to exchange his products against the country merchant's goods and at the end of the year when the time came to settle accounts there was almost nothing coming to him, that is why the sons of our farmers were leaving for the United States, their fathers being unable to give them a start at home, as they are doing to-day. A great number of our farmers were compelled to leave their farm to find work in the American manufactories during the

winter ,season to pay the mortgages on their property.
To prevent such a deplorable state of affairs the only remedy in my judgment was a policy of protection for the manufacturers and a policy of exportation for our natural products. Before 1896, the manufacturers had to curtail their output six months in the year, and to leave without employment a large number of men who had to leave the country.
That is why we had in the city of Montreal 27,000 untenanted dwellings. The building industry was paralyzed and all classes of the population suffered by it, from the lumberman in the woods to the banker in his office. Since the return of prosperity, that is to say since about fifteen years, the population of Montreal has increased by about three hundred thousand inhabitants.
What do we see to-day? The number of the manufactories are continually on the increase, the building industry is in full swing and we can see properous banks at the corner of nearly every street. Everybody seems to be in comfortable circumstances, the day labourer who earned from 80 to 00 cents a day receives to-day two dollars and $2.25 a day. The man with a good trade easy earns four and five dollars a day. I maintain that if the government persists in a policy of protection on natural products, before ten years we will return to the conditions we were in in 1896, and that will endure so long as the country produces enough to maintain a population of two or three hundred millions that we have not.
As I have said, we must have a policy tending to promote exportation of our over production in natural products, because we have not enough population to consume all that the farmers have to sell.
I do not intend to make a speech, but I can say with mv hon. friend from La-prairie, that reciprocity is not buried, it is not even dead.
If the question had been judged on its merits by the electors, if men like Messrs. Bourassa and Lavergne and their Nationalist friends had not misled the people on the naval poilicy, the Liberal party would again be in power to-day, and reciprocity would have carried the day.
As to the naval question, I didn't speak much about it to the electors of St, Mary's division. I merely went to the trouble of explaining that all those clauses that Mr. Bourassa was giving as binding clauses, were only optional. I told the electors that if the Conservative party had been in earnest on the naval policy, they would have resorted to the same tactics as they resorted to on the reciprocity treaty, that is to say, they w'ould have blocked the estimates and Mr. MARTIN (Montreal).
forced the government to go before the people on the naval policy.
To-day the electors of the province of Quebec must perceive that they have been duped. We had the proof of it when the Minister of Public Works himself told us that they had ' played the game.' The stand taken by the government on the question of reciprocity, on the Manitoba school question, on the ' Ne Temere ' decree, has been nothing but a sham, and the electors will soon discover that the Conservatives carried many counties by false representations.
